papers.title: The Unintended Trade-off of AI Alignment:Balancing Hallucination Mitigation and Safety in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do truthfulness-enhancing edits affect jailbreak susceptibility, and which components mediate the truthfulness-safety interaction?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a trade-off between improving truthfulness and maintaining safety in LLMs, and proposes a method using sparse autoencoders to disentangle refusal and hallucination features, preserving the refusal subspace during fine-tuning to mitigate the trade-off.
papers.conclusion: There is a trade-off between truthfulness and refusal alignment in LLMs, and the proposed method using sparse autoencoders to disentangle features and preserve the refusal subspace during fine-tuning can maintain safety while preventing hallucinations from increasing.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness-enhancing edits (e.g., ITI, TruthX) increase jailbreak susceptibility, revealing a trade-off between factuality and safety.
Hallucination and refusal behaviors share overlapping internal representations in specific attention heads.
Fine-tuning on benign datasets can degrade safety alignment due to shared representational space between refusal and hallucination features.
The proposed SAE-guided fine-tuning method preserves refusal behavior while improving task utility, mitigating the trade-off.
papers.limitation:
Further investigation is needed to interpret how different alignment methods affect knowledge suppression and whether their impact varies across model architectures.
The analysis primarily examined specific components; a more comprehensive study of additional layers and mechanisms may yield deeper insights.
The proposed solution relies on a trained SAE, which may limit its practicality for fine-tuning at scale.
papers.abstract: Hallucination in large language models (LLMs) has been widely studied in recent years, with progress in both detection and mitigation aimed at improving truthfulness. Yet, a critical side effect remains largely overlooked: enhancing truthfulness can negatively impact safety alignment. In this paper, we investigate this trade-off and show that increasing factual accuracy often comes at the cost of weakened refusal behavior. Our analysis reveals that this arises from overlapping components in the model that simultaneously encode hallucination and refusal information, leading alignment methods to suppress factual knowledge unintentionally. We further examine how fine-tuning on benign datasets, even when curated for safety, can degrade alignment for the same reason. To address this, we propose a method that disentangles refusal-related features from hallucination features using sparse autoencoders, and preserves refusal behavior during fine-tuning through subspace orthogonalization. This approach prevents hallucinations from increasing while maintaining safety alignment.We evaluate our method on commonsense reasoning tasks and harmful benchmarks (AdvBench and StrongReject). Results demonstrate that our approach preserves refusal behavior and task utility, mitigating the trade-off between truthfulness and safety.

papers.title: Towards Understanding the Fragility of Multilingual LLMs against Fine-Tuning Attacks
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the cross-lingual generalization of fine-tuning attacks in multilingual LLMs and whether safety-related information is language-agnostic.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that fine-tuning attacks on multilingual LLMs generalize across languages, proposes Safety Information Localization (SIL) to identify language-agnostic safety parameters, and shows that modifying only 20% of weights can break safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that multilingual LLMs are vulnerable to cross-lingual fine-tuning attacks due to language-agnostic safety parameters, and proposes SIL as a tool to analyze and understand these vulnerabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning attacks in one language can jailbreak multilingual LLMs across multiple languages.
Safety information in multilingual LLMs is language-agnostic and can be localized with SIL.
Modifying only 20% of weight parameters via SIL can break safety alignment across all languages.
Freezing safety-related parameters does not prevent fine-tuning attacks due to alternative pathways.
The attack vectors identified by SIL can jailbreak LLMs even after language adaptation.
papers.limitation: Harmfulness detector sensitivity may vary across languages, and linguistic characteristics may affect generalization of safety capabilities.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have sparked widespread concerns about their safety. Recent work demonstrates that safety alignment of LLMs can be easily removed by fine-tuning with a few adversarially chosen instruction-following examples, i.e., fine-tuning attacks. We take a further step to understand fine-tuning attacks in multilingual LLMs. We first discover cross-lingual generalization of fine-tuning attacks: using a few adversarially chosen instruction-following examples in one language, multilingual LLMs can also be easily compromised (e.g., multilingual LLMs fail to refuse harmful prompts in other languages). Motivated by this finding, we hypothesize that safety-related information is language-agnostic and propose a new method termed Safety Information Localization (SIL) to identify the safety-related information in the model parameter space. Through SIL, we validate this hypothesis and find that only changing 20% of weight parameters in fine-tuning attacks can break safety alignment across all languages. Furthermore, we provide evidence to the alternative pathways hypothesis for why freezing safety-related parameters does not prevent fine-tuning attacks, and we demonstrate that our attack vector can still jailbreak LLMs adapted to new languages.

papers.title: Surgical Refusal Ablation: Disentangling Safety from Intelligence via Concept-Guided Spectral Cleaning
papers.research_question: How can refusal behavior in safety-aligned language models be ablated without causing collateral damage to core capabilities like math and coding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Surgical Refusal Ablation (SRA), a method that cleans refusal vectors by orthogonalizing against capability and style directions, enabling precise ablation of refusal behavior with minimal distribution drift and preserved capabilities.
papers.conclusion: SRA treats refusal ablation as a semantic disentanglement problem, achieving behavioral editing with dramatically reduced drift and preserved capabilities compared to standard methods.
papers.key_findings:
SRA achieves deep refusal reduction (0–2% on harmful suite) with negligible perplexity impact on wikitext_2_raw and minimal distribution drift.
Standard ablation induces severe distribution drift, while SRA maintains original distribution while achieving low refusal rates.
SRA preserves or improves math and code perplexity on GSM8K and MBPP datasets.
The dirty refusal vector is polysemantic, entangling refusal signals with unrelated linguistic structure and capability circuits.
Cleaning the vector via spectral residualization reduces 'Ghost Noise' damage caused by standard ablation.
papers.limitation:
The atom registry is curated and may miss confounds; unseen entanglers could still leak into the refusal direction.
Evaluation limitations include refusal detection being definition-dependent, finite harmful prompt suites, and proxy drift metrics not substituting for comprehensive behavioral evaluation.
future_direction: Automating atom discovery or expanding registries to handle unseen confounds.
papers.abstract: Safety-aligned language models systematically refuse harmful requests. While activation steering can modulate refusal, ablating the raw "refusal vector" calculated from contrastive harmful and harmless prompts often causes collateral damage and distribution drift. We argue this degradation occurs because the raw vector is polysemantic, entangling the refusal signal with core capability circuits and linguistic style. We introduce Surgical Refusal Ablation (SRA) to distill these steering directions. SRA constructs a registry of independent Concept Atoms representing protected capabilities and stylistic confounds, then uses ridge-regularized spectral residualization to orthogonalize the refusal vector against these directions. This yields a clean refusal direction that targets refusal-relevant structure while minimizing disruption to the model's semantic geometry. Across five models (Qwen3-VL and Ministral series), SRA achieves deep refusal reduction (0-2%) with negligible perplexity impact on Wikitext-2 (mean delta PPL approx. 0.02) and minimal distribution drift. Notably, standard ablation on Qwen3-VL-4B induces severe drift (first-token KL = 2.088), whereas SRA maintains the original distribution (KL = 0.044) while achieving the same 0% refusal rate. Using teacher-forced perplexity on GSM8K and MBPP as a high-resolution capability proxy, we show SRA preserves math and code distributions. These results suggest that common "model damage" is often "Ghost Noise," defined as the spectral bleeding of the dirty refusal direction into capability subspaces.

papers.title: Unraveling and Mitigating Safety Alignment Degradation of Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: What causes safety alignment degradation in Vision-Language Models when vision modules are integrated, and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Cross-Modality Representation Manipulation (CMRM), an inference-time method to mitigate safety alignment degradation in VLMs by calibrating multi-modal representations to align with the LLM backbone's distribution.
papers.conclusion: CMRM effectively recovers safety alignment in VLMs without compromising performance, highlighting the importance of addressing representation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
Safety alignment degrades in VLMs due to representation shift when vision modality is added.
CMRM significantly reduces unsafe rates, e.g., from 61.53% to 3.15% for LLaVA-7B.
CMRM does not compromise general utility of VLMs.
The representation shift can be visualized using PCA and corrected with shifting vectors.
Full layer manipulation is optimal for safety improvement.
papers.limitation:
Increases computational overhead during inference
Focuses only on safety, not other aspects like reasoning or faithfulness
future_direction: Extend to other domains of VLMs such as reasoning ability and faithfulness
Investigate features for optimal anchor dataset
papers.abstract: The safety alignment ability of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) is prone to be degraded by the integration of the vision module compared to its LLM backbone. We investigate this phenomenon, dubbed as ''safety alignment degradation'' in this paper, and show that the challenge arises from the representation gap that emerges when introducing vision modality to VLMs. In particular, we show that the representations of multi-modal inputs shift away from that of text-only inputs which represent the distribution that the LLM backbone is optimized for. At the same time, the safety alignment capabilities, initially developed within the textual embedding space, do not successfully transfer to this new multi-modal representation space. To reduce safety alignment degradation, we introduce Cross-Modality Representation Manipulation (CMRM), an inference time representation intervention method for recovering the safety alignment ability that is inherent in the LLM backbone of VLMs, while simultaneously preserving the functional capabilities of VLMs. The empirical results show that our framework significantly recovers the alignment ability that is inherited from the LLM backbone with minimal impact on the fluency and linguistic capabilities of pre-trained VLMs even without additional training. Specifically, the unsafe rate of LLaVA-7B on multi-modal input can be reduced from 61.53% to as low as 3.15% with only inference-time intervention. WARNING: This paper contains examples of toxic or harmful language.

papers.title: Light Alignment Improves LLM Safety via Model Self-Reflection with a Single Neuron
papers.research_question: How can we design a lightweight safety alignment method that uses a single neuron as a gating mechanism to balance model intrinsic capabilities and external guidance, thereby improving safety without compromising utility?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a lightweight safety alignment method (NGSD) that uses a single neuron as a gating mechanism to balance intrinsic model capabilities with external safety guidance, achieving a favorable safety-utility trade-off with minimal training overhead.
papers.conclusion: Lightweight and targeted safety alignment mechanisms, such as NGSD, can provide meaningful safety improvements without significantly degrading utility, offering a practical direction for deploying safer large language models.
papers.key_findings:
NGSD reduces attack success rates across multiple jailbreak attack scenarios (e.g., GCG, PAIR, AutoDAN).
NGSD preserves utility on benign tasks (e.g., GSM8K, Just-Eval) better than strong baselines like SafeDecoding.
The neuron-based gating mechanism is more robust and responsive than alternative gating methods (EMA, SMG).
The method demonstrates strong generalization and transferability across model scales and families.
NGSD requires only training a small expert model and efficiently transfers to larger models within the same family.
papers.limitation:
Effectiveness in more open-ended or long-horizon settings remains unclear.
Differences in tokenization limit generalization across model families.
future_direction: Explore adaptive risk estimation and more general safety alignment strategies.
Conduct cross-family evaluation under diverse generation regimes.
papers.abstract: The safety of large language models (LLMs) has increasingly emerged as a fundamental aspect of their development. Existing safety alignment for LLMs is predominantly achieved through post-training methods, which are computationally expensive and often fail to generalize well across different models. A small number of lightweight alignment approaches either rely heavily on prior-computed safety injections or depend excessively on the model's own capabilities, resulting in limited generalization and degraded efficiency and usability during generation. In this work, we propose a safety-aware decoding method that requires only low-cost training of an expert model and employs a single neuron as a gating mechanism. By effectively balancing the model's intrinsic capabilities with external guidance, our approach simultaneously preserves utility and enhances output safety. It demonstrates clear advantages in training overhead and generalization across model scales, offering a new perspective on lightweight alignment for the safe and practical deployment of large language models. Code: https://github.com/Beijing-AISI/NGSD.

papers.title: Safety Layers in Aligned Large Language Models: The Key to LLM Security
papers.research_question: What is the internal mechanism (safety layers) that enables aligned LLMs to recognize malicious queries, and how can we fine-tune these models without degrading their security?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies safety layers in aligned LLMs that are crucial for security and proposes SPPFT, a fine-tuning method that freezes these layers to preserve security while maintaining performance.
papers.conclusion: Safety layers are the key to LLM security, and freezing them during fine-tuning via SPPFT effectively prevents security degradation while preserving performance.
papers.key_findings:
Aligned LLMs contain a small set of contiguous middle layers, called safety layers, that are crucial for distinguishing malicious from normal queries.
Safety layers emerge as a result of security alignment; pre-trained LLMs do not exhibit such layers.
Scaling the parameters of safety layers amplifies or diminishes the model's security, as measured by over-rejection.
The proposed SPPFT method, which freezes safety layers during fine-tuning, significantly preserves security while maintaining performance and reducing computational cost.
Freezing layers other than the safety layers does not effectively protect security, confirming the specificity of safety layers.
papers.abstract: Aligned LLMs are secure, capable of recognizing and refusing to answer malicious questions. However, the role of internal parameters in maintaining such security is not well understood yet, further these models can be vulnerable to security degradation when subjected to fine-tuning attacks. To address these challenges, our work uncovers the mechanism behind security in aligned LLMs at the parameter level, identifying a small set of contiguous layers in the middle of the model that are crucial for distinguishing malicious queries from normal ones, referred to as ``safety layers". We first confirm the existence of these safety layers by analyzing variations in input vectors within the model's internal layers. Additionally, we leverage the over-rejection phenomenon and parameters scaling analysis to precisely locate the safety layers. Building on these findings, we propose a novel fine-tuning approach, Safely Partial-Parameter Fine-Tuning (SPPFT), that fixes the gradient of the safety layers during fine-tuning to address the security degradation. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly preserve LLM security while maintaining performance and reducing computational resources compared to full fine-tuning.

papers.title: Safety Alignment via Constrained Knowledge Unlearning
papers.research_question: How can we improve the safety alignment of large language models against jailbreak attacks by unlearning harmful knowledge while preserving useful knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Constrained Knowledge Unlearning (CKU), a safety alignment method that identifies and fixes knowledge-related neurons in MLP layers during unlearning to remove harmful knowledge while preserving model utility.
papers.conclusion: CKU effectively enhances LLM safety against jailbreak attacks by unlearning harmful knowledge while preserving general capabilities, offering a promising approach for safety alignment and knowledge editing.
papers.key_findings:
CKU achieves a superior balance between safety and utility compared to existing methods like RSFT, GAM, Eraser, Safe Unlearning, and Circuit Break.
Fixing 80% of neurons (Neuron Locking Rate=0.8) during unlearning yields the greatest safety improvement.
Unlearning applied only to a subset of MLP layers (layers 8-12) results in a fourfold increase in safety with only a 0.15% reduction in utility.
The neuron selection mechanism based on SNIP scoring is more effective than random selection for preserving utility during unlearning.
The unlearning regularization parameter λ controls the safety-utility trade-off, with λ=1.5 providing an optimal balance.
papers.limitation:
CKU's effectiveness varies across different domains or datasets.
CKU may occasionally struggle to provide nuanced explanations in highly complex or ambiguous contexts.
papers.abstract: Despite significant progress in safety alignment, large language models (LLMs) remain susceptible to jailbreak attacks. Existing defense mechanisms have not fully deleted harmful knowledge in LLMs, which allows such attacks to bypass safeguards and produce harmful outputs. To address this challenge, we propose a novel safety alignment strategy, Constrained Knowledge Unlearning (CKU), which focuses on two primary objectives: knowledge localization and retention, and unlearning harmful knowledge. CKU works by scoring neurons in specific multilayer perceptron (MLP) layers to identify a subset U of neurons associated with useful knowledge. During the unlearning process, CKU prunes the gradients of neurons in U to preserve valuable knowledge while effectively mitigating harmful content. Experimental results demonstrate that CKU significantly enhances model safety without compromising overall performance, offering a superior balance between safety and utility compared to existing methods. Additionally, our analysis of neuron knowledge sensitivity across various MLP layers provides valuable insights into the mechanics of safety alignment and model knowledge editing.

papers.title: No Two Devils Alike: Unveiling Distinct Mechanisms of Fine-tuning Attacks
papers.research_question: While different fine-tuning attacks can all significantly compromise safety, do their attack mechanisms exhibit strong similarities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that two representative fine-tuning attacks (Explicit Harmful Attack and Identity-Shifting Attack) have distinct mechanisms for compromising an LLM's safety alignment, indicating the need for diverse defense strategies.
papers.conclusion: Different fine-tuning attacks exploit distinct mechanisms to compromise LLM safety, underscoring the need for varied and robust defense strategies.
papers.key_findings:
EHA aggressively disrupts the harmful instruction recognition stage by suppressing the transmission of harmful signals in upper layers, while ISA does not significantly impact this stage.
Both EHA and ISA disrupt the initial refusal tone generation, but EHA suppresses refusal tokens via MLPs in mid-layers, whereas ISA does not.
Both attacks impair the refusal response completion stage, with ISA having a greater impact, causing the model to persistently generate harmful content even with refusal prefixes.
Adding a safety-oriented system prompt only partially mitigates the impairment caused by the attacks.
The attacks cause representation shifts: EHA shifts representations more for harmful inputs, while ISA causes a shift orthogonal to the harmfulness direction.
papers.limitation:
The study only investigates two fine-tuning attacks (EHA and ISA), which do not encompass the full spectrum of possible attacks.
The analysis is conducted solely on Llama-2-7b-chat, limiting the generalizability of the findings to other models.
The investigation does not involve the mechanics of particular components (e.g., individual attention heads) due to scope constraints.
future_direction: Using trained probes at mid-layers to robustly detect harmful inputs without an external detector.
Developing more attack-resisting model manipulation methods for safeguarding, as current steering methods may be less effective on attacked models.
papers.abstract: The existing safety alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) is found fragile and could be easily attacked through different strategies, such as through fine-tuning on a few harmful examples or manipulating the prefix of the generation results. However, the attack mechanisms of these strategies are still underexplored. In this paper, we ask the following question: \textit{while these approaches can all significantly compromise safety, do their attack mechanisms exhibit strong similarities?} To answer this question, we break down the safeguarding process of an LLM when encountered with harmful instructions into three stages: (1) recognizing harmful instructions, (2) generating an initial refusing tone, and (3) completing the refusal response. Accordingly, we investigate whether and how different attack strategies could influence each stage of this safeguarding process. We utilize techniques such as logit lens and activation patching to identify model components that drive specific behavior, and we apply cross-model probing to examine representation shifts after an attack. In particular, we analyze the two most representative types of attack approaches: Explicit Harmful Attack (EHA) and Identity-Shifting Attack (ISA). Surprisingly, we find that their attack mechanisms diverge dramatically. Unlike ISA, EHA tends to aggressively target the harmful recognition stage. While both EHA and ISA disrupt the latter two stages, the extent and mechanisms of their attacks differ significantly. Our findings underscore the importance of understanding LLMs' internal safeguarding process and suggest that diverse defense mechanisms are required to effectively cope with various types of attacks.

papers.title: Soteria: Language-Specific Functional Parameter Steering for Multilingual Safety Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we ensure consistent safety across multiple languages in large language models by locating and minimally adjusting language-specific functional parameters?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Soteria, a lightweight method that identifies and adjusts language-specific functional attention heads to improve multilingual safety alignment by modifying only ~3% of parameters, reducing harmful outputs without degrading overall model performance.
papers.conclusion: Soteria provides an effective, parameter-efficient path to scalable multilingual safety alignment, enhancing model safety across diverse languages without compromising utility.
papers.key_findings:
Soteria significantly reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) across high-, mid-, and low-resource languages on safety benchmarks like MultiJail and XThreatBench.
The method outperforms baseline safety alignment techniques such as Safety Arithmetic, Resta, and TIES.
Modifying only the O-projection weights of identified functional heads preserves general model capabilities, as shown by stable MMLU scores.
Attention head analysis reveals that high- and mid-resource languages share functional heads in mid-layers, while low-resource languages utilize heads in later layers.
The approach is robust against state-of-the-art jailbreak attacks like POATE and RDR.
papers.limitation:
Relies on per-language functional neuron identification, which requires accurate language segmentation and task-based data in each target language; resource constraints and data limitations can reduce selection precision.
Does not guarantee comprehensive coverage of every cultural nuance or emergent harmful behavior.
future_direction: Investigating attention-head analysis to tackle task-specific heads, misalignment, and hallucination issues.
Enhancing universal attention heads to improve cross-lingual understanding and zero-shot performance for underrepresented languages.
Refining or shifting the latent space of problematic heads to improve overall alignment and trustworthiness.
papers.abstract: Ensuring consistent safety across multiple languages remains a significant challenge for large language models (LLMs). We introduce Soteria, a lightweight yet powerful strategy that locates and minimally adjusts the "functional heads" most responsible for harmful content generation in each language. By altering only a fraction of parameters, Soteria drastically reduces policy violations without sacrificing overall model performance, even in low-resource settings. To rigorously evaluate our approach, we also present XThreatBench, a specialized multilingual dataset capturing fine-grained harmful behaviors drawn from real policy guidelines. Experiments with leading open-source LLMs (e.g., Llama, Qwen, Mistral) show that Soteria consistently improves safety metrics across high-, mid-, and low-resource languages. These findings highlight a promising path toward scalable, linguistically attuned, and ethically aligned LLMs worldwide.

papers.title: Safety at One Shot: Patching Fine-Tuned LLMs with A Single Instance
papers.research_question: How can we recover model safety with minimal cost, without sacrificing utility?
papers.core_contribution: Safety alignment in fine-tuned LLMs can be fully recovered with a single safe instance, without sacrificing utility, due to the low-rank structure of the safety gradient.
papers.conclusion: One-shot safety recovery is a simple, efficient, and effective method to restore safety alignment in fine-tuned LLMs, enabled by the low-rank nature of safety gradients.
papers.key_findings:
Safety alignment can be restored with a single safe instance, regardless of the amount of harmful fine-tuning data or model size.
The safety gradient lies in a low-rank subspace, explaining the efficiency of one-shot recovery.
Recovery converges within a few epochs, independent of model size and harmful fine-tuning scale.
General safety data is more effective for one-shot recovery than category-specific data.
The method is effective across diverse model families (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, GPT) and adversarial fine-tuning scenarios.
future_direction: Developing principled defenses against adaptive adversaries
Understanding the broader geometry of safety gradients
Integrating one-shot recovery into practical safety monitoring pipelines for real-world deployment
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) can substantially compromise their safety. Previous approaches require many safety samples or calibration sets, which not only incur significant computational overhead during realignment but also lead to noticeable degradation in model utility. Contrary to this belief, we show that safety alignment can be fully recovered with only a single safety example, without sacrificing utility and at minimal cost. Remarkably, this recovery is effective regardless of the number of harmful examples used in fine-tuning or the size of the underlying model, and convergence is achieved within just a few epochs. Furthermore, we uncover the low-rank structure of the safety gradient, which explains why such efficient correction is possible. We validate our findings across five safety-aligned LLMs and multiple datasets, demonstrating the generality of our approach.

papers.title: Anchoring Refusal Direction: Mitigating Safety Risks in Tuning via Projection Constraint
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate safety risks posed by Instruction Fine-Tuning (IFT) while preserving task performance gains?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a projection-constraint method (ProCon) that stabilizes the refusal direction in LLM hidden states during instruction fine-tuning, effectively mitigating associated safety risks without compromising task performance.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that anchoring the refusal direction via a projection constraint method effectively mitigates safety risks introduced by instruction fine-tuning, providing an interpretability-driven approach for safer LLM tuning.
papers.key_findings:
The refusal direction (r-direction), a key representation for safety, drifts during instruction fine-tuning, which is identified as a primary cause of emerging safety risks.
Applying a projection constraint on hidden states along the r-direction can mitigate this drift and reduce safety risks.
A warm-up strategy that applies strong constraints in early training stages and broadening the data distribution with safety-oriented samples further enhances the method's effectiveness and stability.
The proposed ProCon method, especially the enhanced ProCon_wu_safe variant, consistently outperforms strong baselines in mitigating safety risks across various LLMs and scenarios while preserving task performance.
papers.abstract: Instruction Fine-Tuning (IFT) has been widely adopted as an effective post-training strategy to enhance various abilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, prior studies have shown that IFT can significantly compromise LLMs' safety, particularly their ability to refuse malicious instructions, raising significant concerns. Recent research into the internal mechanisms of LLMs has identified the refusal direction (r-direction) in the hidden states, which plays a pivotal role in governing refusal behavior. Building on this insight, our study reveals that the r-direction tends to drift during training, which we identify as one of the causes of the associated safety risks. To mitigate such drift, our proposed ProCon method introduces a projection-constrained loss term that regularizes the projection magnitude of each training sample's hidden state onto the r-direction. Our initial analysis shows that applying an appropriate constraint can effectively mitigate the refusal direction drift and associated safety risks, but remains limited by overall performance barriers. To overcome this barrier, informed by our observation of early-stage sharp drift and a data-driven perspective, we introduce a warm-up strategy that emphasizes early-stage strong constraints and broaden the data distribution to strengthen constraint signals, leading to an enhanced ProCon method. Experimental results under various datasets, scenarios, and LLMs demonstrate that our method can significantly mitigate safety risks posed by IFT while preserving task performance gains. Even compared with strong baselines, our method consistently delivers superior overall performance. Crucially, our analysis indicates that ProCon can contribute to stabilizing the r-direction during training, while such an interpretability-driven exploration of LLMs' internal mechanisms lays a solid foundation for future safety research.

papers.title: Safety Alignment as Continual Learning: Mitigating the Alignment Tax via Orthogonal Gradient Projection
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate the alignment tax (safety post-training reducing general utility) in LLMs by reframing safety alignment as a continual learning problem and using orthogonal gradient projection?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes OGPSA, a lightweight gradient projection method that decouples safety optimization from capability forgetting by projecting safety gradients onto the orthogonal complement of a learned general capability subspace, effectively mitigating the alignment tax.
papers.conclusion: OGPSA provides a scalable and effective solution to the alignment tax by explicitly decoupling safety updates from capability-preserving parameter directions, achieving a superior trade-off between safety and general abilities.
papers.key_findings:
OGPSA consistently improves the safety–utility Pareto frontier over standard baselines across SFT, DPO, and sequential SFT→DPO settings.
On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct under SFT→DPO, OGPSA recovers general capability: SimpleQA from 0.53% to 3.03% and IFEval from 51.94% to 63.96% while maintaining strong safety.
OGPSA is data-efficient, requiring only small reference datasets (e.g., 100-200 samples per capability dimension) to estimate the general capability subspace.
OGPSA scales effectively across model sizes from 0.5B to 7B parameters.
Dynamic updating of the capability subspace (every K steps) is essential for optimal performance, outperforming static subspaces.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often incur an alignment tax: safety post-training can reduce general utility (e.g., reasoning and coding). We argue that this tax primarily arises from continual-learning-style forgetting in sequential alignment, where distribution shift and conflicting objectives cause safety updates to overwrite pre-trained competencies. Accordingly, we cast safety alignment as a continual learning (CL) problem that must balance plasticity (acquiring safety constraints) and stability (preserving general abilities). We propose Orthogonal Gradient Projection for Safety Alignment (OGPSA), a lightweight method that mitigates interference by constraining each safety update to be orthogonal (in a first-order sense) to a learned subspace capturing general capabilities. Specifically, OGPSA estimates a low-rank capability subspace from gradients on a small reference set and projects the safety gradient onto its orthogonal complement before updating. This produces safety-directed updates that minimally perturb prior knowledge while retaining capacity for alignment. OGPSA is plug-and-play and integrates into standard post-training pipelines without large-scale replay, auxiliary objectives, or retraining. Across Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and sequential SFT$\rightarrow$DPO settings, OGPSA consistently improves the safety--utility Pareto frontier over standard baselines. For instance, on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct under SFT$\rightarrow$DPO, OGPSA preserves strong safety while recovering general capability, improving SimpleQA from 0.53\% to 3.03\% and IFEval from 51.94\% to 63.96\%. Our source code is available at \href{https://github.com/SunGL001/OGPSA}{OGPSA}

papers.title: Self-Aware Safety Augmentation: Leveraging Internal Semantic Understanding to Enhance Safety in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal dynamics of safety perception, semantic understanding, and linguistic expression in LVLMs, and how can they be leveraged to enhance safety without fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Self-Aware Safety Augmentation (SASA), a tuning-free method that enhances safety in LVLMs by projecting semantic-rich representations from intermediate fused layers onto earlier safety-critical layers, leveraging the model's internal understanding.
papers.conclusion: SASA effectively enhances LVLM safety by projecting semantic-rich representations to early safety layers, achieving high safety performance with minimal data and no tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Safety mechanisms are predominantly concentrated in early layers; ablating top-5 safety heads increases ASR by an average of 47%.
Semantic understanding progressively matures in intermediate layers, enabling internal discrimination between harmful and benign inputs, but this discriminative power diminishes in deeper layers due to alignment constraints.
The model possesses internal risk awareness that is not consistently translated into its language output.
SASA reduces ASR by an average of 97% using only 5% of data, with minimal degradation of helpfulness.
SASA exhibits remarkable zero-shot generalization capabilities on previously unseen datasets.
future_direction: Future work could explore extending SASA to other modalities and tasks, and investigating the interplay between safety and other model capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) are vulnerable to harmful input compared to their language-only backbones. We investigated this vulnerability by exploring LVLMs internal dynamics, framing their inherent safety understanding in terms of three key capabilities. Specifically, we define these capabilities as safety perception, semantic understanding, and alignment for linguistic expression, and experimentally pinpointed their primary locations within the model architecture. The results indicate that safety perception often emerges before comprehensive semantic understanding, leading to the reduction in safety. Motivated by these findings, we propose \textbf{Self-Aware Safety Augmentation (SASA)}, a technique that projects informative semantic representations from intermediate layers onto earlier safety-oriented layers. This approach leverages the model's inherent semantic understanding to enhance safety recognition without fine-tuning. Then, we employ linear probing to articulate the model's internal semantic comprehension to detect the risk before the generation process. Extensive experiments on various datasets and tasks demonstrate that SASA significantly improves the safety of LVLMs, with minimal impact on the utility.

papers.title: Who Transfers Safety? Identifying and Targeting Cross-Lingual Shared Safety Neurons
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the neural mechanisms underlying cross-lingual safety alignment in LLMs, specifically identifying a sparse set of shared safety neurons that regulate safety behavior across languages.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a sparse set of cross-lingual shared safety neurons (SS-Neurons) that regulate safety behavior across languages and proposes a neuron-oriented training strategy that selectively fine-tunes these neurons to improve safety in low-resource languages without degrading general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that cross-lingual safety alignment can be achieved by identifying and selectively fine-tuning a sparse set of shared safety neurons, which improves safety in low-resource languages while minimizing the alignment tax.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs contain monolingual safety neurons (MS-Neurons) that are causally responsible for safety refusal behavior.
The subset of MS-Neurons shared between high-resource and low-resource languages (SS-Neurons) serves as a bridge for cross-lingual safety transfer.
Suppressing SS-Neurons causes concurrent safety drops across low-resource languages, while reinforcing them improves cross-lingual defensive consistency.
The proposed SS-Neuron expansion strategy, which fine-tunes only the English MS-Neurons using parallel safety data, significantly reduces attack success rates in low-resource languages while preserving model utility.
The method is parameter-efficient, updating less than 0.6% of parameters, and outperforms state-of-the-art safety alignment methods.
papers.limitation: The study primarily focuses on safety-oriented tasks, and the applicability to general-purpose tasks remains to be explored.
future_direction: Validate the neuron-level intervention across non-safety domains to transfer complex cognitive skills.
papers.abstract: Multilingual safety remains significantly imbalanced, leaving non-high-resource (NHR) languages vulnerable compared to robust high-resource (HR) ones. Moreover, the neural mechanisms driving safety alignment remain unclear despite observed cross-lingual representation transfer. In this paper, we find that LLMs contain a set of cross-lingual shared safety neurons (SS-Neurons), a remarkably small yet critical neuronal subset that jointly regulates safety behavior across languages. We first identify monolingual safety neurons (MS-Neurons) and validate their causal role in safety refusal behavior through targeted activation and suppression. Our cross-lingual analyses then identify SS-Neurons as the subset of MS-Neurons shared between HR and NHR languages, serving as a bridge to transfer safety capabilities from HR to NHR domains. We observe that suppressing these neurons causes concurrent safety drops across NHR languages, whereas reinforcing them improves cross-lingual defensive consistency. Building on these insights, we propose a simple neuron-oriented training strategy that targets SS-Neurons based on language resource distribution and model architecture. Experiments demonstrate that fine-tuning this tiny neuronal subset outperforms state-of-the-art methods, significantly enhancing NHR safety while maintaining the model's general capabilities. The code and dataset will be available athttps://github.com/1518630367/SS-Neuron-Expansion.

papers.title: Revisiting Robustness for LLM Safety Alignment via Selective Geometry Control
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether robustness failures in LLM safety alignment can be addressed by data-centric methods alone, and proposes a geometry-aware optimization framework to improve robustness under domain shift and noisy supervision.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ShaPO, a geometry-aware preference optimization framework that selectively stabilizes safety-critical parameter directions to improve robustness under domain shift and noisy supervision.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that optimization geometry is a complementary axis for robust LLM safety alignment, and ShaPO effectively improves robustness by selectively stabilizing safety-critical parameter directions.
papers.key_findings:
ShaPO consistently improves safety robustness over popular preference optimization methods across diverse safety benchmarks and noisy preference settings.
ShaPO composes cleanly with data-robust objectives, yielding additional gains.
Selective geometry control avoids over-regularization and improves cross-domain robustness compared to uniform control.
Token-level and reward-level ShaPO both improve robustness, with reward-level ShaPO offering additional stability under noisy supervision.
Perturbing a small fraction of safety-critical neurons accounts for most of the worst-case alignment loss, justifying selective control.
papers.limitation:
ShaPO introduces additional computational overhead due to geometry-aware optimization.
Identification of alignment-critical directions is based on approximate signals (linear probe).
future_direction: Improving the efficiency and scalability of geometry-aware optimization for larger-scale models.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment of large language models remains brittle under domain shift and noisy preference supervision. Most existing robust alignment methods focus on uncertainty in alignment data, while overlooking optimization-induced fragility in preference-based objectives. In this work, we revisit robustness for LLM safety alignment from an optimization geometry perspective, and argue that robustness failures cannot be addressed by data-centric methods alone. We propose ShaPO, a geometry-aware preference optimization framework that enforces worst-case alignment objectives via selective geometry control over alignment-critical parameter subspace. By avoiding uniform geometry constraints, ShaPO mitigates the over-regularization that can harm robustness under distribution shift. We instantiate ShaPO at two levels: token-level ShaPO stabilizes likelihood-based surrogate optimization, while reward-level ShaPO enforces reward-consistent optimization under noisy supervision. Across diverse safety benchmarks and noisy preference settings, ShaPO consistently improves safety robustness over popular preference optimization methods. Moreover, ShaPO composes cleanly with data-robust objectives, yielding additional gains and empirically supporting the proposed optimization-geometry perspective.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of LoRA-Adapted Language Models for Nuclear Reactor Safety Applications
papers.research_question: How does LoRA adaptation alter neuron activation patterns in an LLM for a nuclear reactor safety domain, and what is the causal role of these altered neurons?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents a methodology for tracing domain expertise in a LoRA-adapted LLM to a sparse set of neurons and demonstrates that the model's expertise is an emergent property of a neural circuit, providing a pathway for nuclear-grade AI assurance.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates a replicable methodology for moving beyond treating LLMs as opaque black boxes towards a mechanistic understanding of their function, offering a pathway to achieve nuclear-grade AI assurance by identifying, monitoring, and causally testing knowledge-bearing neural circuits.
papers.key_findings:
LoRA fine-tuning on a BWR dataset induced systematic changes in the activation patterns of a small set of neurons in the final MLP layer.
Silencing the entire group of six key neurons collectively caused a statistically significant degradation in BLEU score, while silencing most individual neurons did not, supporting a circuit-based view of knowledge encoding.
Qualitative analysis revealed distinct functional roles for key neurons, such as encoding core technical concepts (#1066, #1086), suppressing generalist language (#941), and representing procedural logic (#176).
The adapted model produced more concise and precise answers than the base model, as measured by a decrease in average answer length and an increase in BLEU score.
The findings suggest that verifying the integrity of distributed neural circuits, rather than individual components, is crucial for safety assurance in nuclear applications.
papers.limitation: The reliance on the BLEU score, while justified for measuring output precision, does not verify factual accuracy.
future_direction: Development of domain-specific evaluation metrics that can automatically verify technical correctness against a trusted knowledge base.
Extending the methodology to other critical nuclear systems, including Pressurized Water Reactors (PWRs) and advanced reactor designs.
Validating the approach across different model architectures, model scales, and technical documentation corpora.
papers.abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into safety-critical domains, such as nuclear engineering, necessitates a deep understanding of their internal reasoning processes. This paper presents a novel methodology for interpreting how an LLM encodes and utilizes domain-specific knowledge, using a Boiling Water Reactor system as a case study. We adapted a general-purpose LLM (Gemma-3-1b-it) to the nuclear domain using a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique known as Low-Rank Adaptation. By comparing the neuron activation patterns of the base model to those of the fine-tuned model, we identified a sparse set of neurons whose behavior was significantly altered during the adaptation process. To probe the causal role of these specialized neurons, we employed a neuron silencing technique. Our results demonstrate that while silencing most of these specialized neurons individually did not produce a statistically significant effect, deactivating the entire group collectively led to a statistically significant degradation in task performance. Qualitative analysis further revealed that silencing these neurons impaired the model's ability to generate detailed, contextually accurate technical information. This paper provides a concrete methodology for enhancing the transparency of an opaque black-box model, allowing domain expertise to be traced to verifiable neural circuits. This offers a pathway towards achieving nuclear-grade artificial intelligence (AI) assurance, addressing the verification and validation challenges mandated by nuclear regulatory frameworks (e.g., 10 CFR 50 Appendix B), which have limited AI deployment in safety-critical nuclear operations.

papers.title: Probing the Robustness of Large Language Models Safety to Latent Perturbations
papers.research_question: What is the robustness of safety alignment in large language models to latent perturbations, and can minor shifts in internal representations trigger unsafe responses?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a fundamental lack of local robustness in the latent representations of safety-aligned LLMs, introduces a probing method and attack (ASA) to exploit this, and proposes a defense (LAPT) that improves robustness without harming general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Current safety alignment methods lack local robustness in the internal representational space, and robust AI safety requires fortifying internal representations rather than just modifying input-output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Minor perturbations to hidden activations can successfully jailbreak safety-aligned LLMs, revealing shallow alignment.
The Activation Steering Attack (ASA) is an effective, lightweight jailbreak method that generalizes across models.
A gradient-based variant (ASAgrad) is even more effective by using harmful suffixes as targets.
Vulnerabilities are concentrated in specific 'fragile layers' within models.
Layer-wise Adversarial Patch Training (LAPT) can enhance alignment robustness against such latent attacks while preserving general task performance.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment is a key requirement for building reliable Artificial General Intelligence. Despite significant advances in safety alignment, we observe that minor latent shifts can still trigger unsafe responses in aligned models. We argue that this stems from the shallow nature of existing alignment methods, which focus on surface-level refusal behaviors without sufficiently altering internal representations. Consequently, small shifts in hidden activations can re-trigger harmful behaviors embedded in the latent space. To explore the robustness of safety alignment to latent perturbations, we introduce a probing method that measures the Negative Log-Likelihood of the original response generated by the model. This probe quantifies local sensitivity in the latent space, serving as a diagnostic tool for identifying vulnerable directions. Based on this signal, we construct effective jailbreak trajectories, giving rise to the Activation Steering Attack (ASA). More importantly, these insights offer a principled foundation for improving alignment robustness. To this end, we introduce Layer-wise Adversarial Patch Training~(LAPT), a fine-tuning strategy that inject controlled perturbations into hidden representations during training. Experimental results highlight that LAPT strengthen alignment robustness without compromising general capabilities. Our findings reveal fundamental flaws in current alignment paradigms and call for representation-level training strategies that move beyond surface-level behavior supervision. Codes and results are available at https://github.com/Carol-gutianle/LatentSafety.

papers.title: Separate the Wheat from the Chaff: A Post-Hoc Approach to Safety Re-Alignment for Fine-Tuned Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we perform safety realignment for fine-tuned language models to restore safety without degrading downstream task performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces IRR, a post-hoc safety realignment method that identifies and removes unsafe delta parameters from fine-tuned models and recalibrates the retained parameters to restore safety while preserving downstream task performance.
papers.conclusion: IRR is an effective safety realignment method that reduces the safety risks of fine-tuned models while maintaining their downstream task performance.
papers.key_findings:
IRR significantly improves model safety on harmful query benchmarks and jailbreak attacks while maintaining downstream task performance, achieving Pareto improvements.
IRR is effective across different fine-tuning methods (full fine-tuning and LoRA) and different models (Llama-2 and Llama-3).
Ablation studies show that the identification step (using safety interference and safety importance) and the recalibration step are crucial for balancing safety and performance.
IRR improves safety across multiple languages (English, Chinese, Vietnamese) in fine-tuned models.
IRR remains effective even when using different safety vectors or when fine-tuning data includes harmful examples.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were not conducted on multimodal models.
The approach for obtaining safety vectors and evaluating safety importance scores is relatively simple and could be improved.
future_direction: Extend the method to multimodal models.
Develop more robust and precise methods for obtaining safety vectors and evaluating safety importance scores.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) achieve effective safety alignment at the time of release, they still face various safety challenges. A key issue is that fine-tuning often compromises the safety alignment of LLMs. To address this issue, we propose a method named IRR (Identify, Remove, and Recalibrate for Safety Realignment) that performs safety realignment for LLMs. The core of IRR is to identify and remove unsafe delta parameters from the fine-tuned models, while recalibrating the retained ones. We evaluate the effectiveness of IRR across various datasets, including both full fine-tuning and LoRA methods. Our results demonstrate that IRR significantly enhances the safety performance of fine-tuned models on safety benchmarks, such as harmful queries and jailbreak attacks, while maintaining their performance on downstream tasks. The source code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/IRR-BD4F.

papers.title: SaLoRA: Safety-Alignment Preserved Low-Rank Adaptation
papers.research_question: What is the reason for safety alignment drop after LoRA fine-tuning, and how can we preserve safety alignment during low-rank adaptation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SaLoRA, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that preserves safety alignment by introducing a fixed safety module and task-specific initialization for low-rank adapters.
papers.conclusion: SaLoRA effectively preserves safety alignment during LoRA fine-tuning while maintaining performance on downstream tasks.
papers.key_findings:
LoRA fine-tuning significantly alters the safety features of LLMs, leading to a drop in safety alignment.
SaLoRA, with its fixed safety module and task-specific initialization, preserves safety alignment while achieving comparable or better downstream task performance.
SaLoRA outperforms existing PEFT methods (LoRA, DoRA, PiSSA) and post-hoc alignment methods (Self-Reminder, InferAligner, Vaccine, Safe LoRA) in terms of harmful rate and utility.
Task-specific initialization for SaLoRA adapters improves convergence and performance compared to standard initialization.
SaLoRA maintains safety alignment even under jailbreak attacks (multi-GCG attack).
papers.abstract: As advancements in large language models (LLMs) continue and the demand for personalized models increases, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods (e.g., LoRA) will become essential due to their efficiency in reducing computation costs. However, recent studies have raised alarming concerns that LoRA fine-tuning could potentially compromise the safety alignment in LLMs, posing significant risks for the model owner. In this paper, we first investigate the underlying mechanism by analyzing the changes in safety alignment related features before and after fine-tuning. Then, we propose a fixed safety module calculated by safety data and a task-specific initialization for trainable parameters in low-rank adaptations, termed Safety-alignment preserved Low-Rank Adaptation (SaLoRA). Unlike previous LoRA methods and their variants, SaLoRA enables targeted modifications to LLMs without disrupting their original alignments. Our experiments show that SaLoRA outperforms various adapters-based approaches across various evaluation metrics in different fine-tuning tasks.

papers.title: Mechanistically analyzing the effects of fine-tuning on procedurally defined tasks
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning alter the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining? Does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning rarely alters a model's underlying capabilities; instead, it typically learns a minimal 'wrapper' transformation on top of existing capabilities. These wrapped capabilities can be sample-efficiently revived via further fine-tuning on relevant tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning primarily learns minimal wrapper transformations over existing model capabilities rather than creating or deleting them, which has implications for safety as wrappers can be easily removed or bypassed.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning alters pretraining capabilities by minimally transforming them via a learned 'wrapper'.
Wrappers are often extremely localized; pruning a few neurons can cause the model to revert to its pretraining capability.
Further fine-tuning on a subset of pretraining data leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the original capability.
When a weakly relevant pretraining capability is present, the model exploits spurious correlations in the fine-tuning data via the wrapper.
The presence and strength of a pretraining capability (influenced by its sampling probability during pretraining) significantly affects fine-tuning dynamics and wrapper formation.
papers.limitation: The analysis is conducted primarily in synthetic, controlled settings (Tracr and PCFGs), which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world fine-tuning scenarios.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex and realistic tasks and models.
Investigating the societal implications of the findings, particularly regarding the safety of fine-tuned models.
Exploring whether the wrapper phenomenon generalizes to other model adaptation methods beyond standard fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large pre-trained models has become the de facto strategy for developing both task-specific and general-purpose machine learning systems, including developing models that are safe to deploy. Despite its clear importance, there has been minimal work that explains how fine-tuning alters the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining: does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones? We address this question empirically in synthetic, controlled settings where we can use mechanistic interpretability tools (e.g., network pruning and probing) to understand how the model's underlying capabilities are changing. We perform an extensive analysis of the effects of fine-tuning in these settings, and show that: (i) fine-tuning rarely alters the underlying model capabilities; (ii) a minimal transformation, which we call a 'wrapper', is typically learned on top of the underlying model capabilities, creating the illusion that they have been modified; and (iii) further fine-tuning on a task where such hidden capabilities are relevant leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the capability, i.e., the model begins reusing these capability after only a few gradient steps. This indicates that practitioners can unintentionally remove a model's safety wrapper merely by fine-tuning it on a, e.g., superficially unrelated, downstream task. We additionally perform analysis on language models trained on the TinyStories dataset to support our claims in a more realistic setup.

papers.title: SCANS: Mitigating the Exaggerated Safety for LLMs via Safety-Conscious Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How to mitigate the exaggerated safety concerns in aligned Large Language Models (LLMs) that cause false refusal of benign queries, without compromising their defense capability against harmful queries?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SCANS, a training-free activation steering method that extracts refusal steering vectors from model hidden states and steers activations in safety-critical layers to reduce false refusal on benign queries while maintaining refusal on harmful ones.
papers.conclusion: SCANS effectively mitigates the exaggerated safety issue in aligned LLMs through activation steering in safety-critical layers, balancing helpfulness and harmlessness without significant degradation of general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
SCANS significantly reduces the false refusal rate on safe prompts (e.g., by 24.7% on XSTest and 26.3% on OKTest on average) without compromising adequate safety on harmful prompts.
The method identifies middle layers as safety-critical for steering, as vocabulary projection of steering vectors from these layers promotes refusal-related tokens.
SCANS has minimal impact on general model capabilities (perplexity, summarization, QA accuracy) and requires minor extra inference cost.
A similarity-based classification method using hidden state transitions effectively distinguishes harmful from benign queries, achieving high F1 scores.
The performance of SCANS is robust across different model sizes and architectures, including Llama2, Vicuna, Qwen, Llama3, and Gemma2.
papers.limitation:
Classification inaccuracy in the steering direction identification can lead to a slight drop in refusal rate on unsafe prompts.
Comparison experiments on larger-scale models (>13B parameters) were limited to one prompt engineering baseline due to computational constraints and time.
Applying too large a steering multiplier (α) can sometimes result in nonsense or repetitive outputs.
future_direction: Improving the classification method for more accurate harmfulness detection.
Conducting more comprehensive comparison experiments on larger-scale models.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment is indispensable for Large Language Models (LLMs) to defend threats from malicious instructions. However, recent researches reveal safety-aligned LLMs prone to reject benign queries due to the exaggerated safety issue, limiting their helpfulness. In this paper, we propose a Safety-Conscious Activation Steering (SCANS) method to mitigate the exaggerated safety concerns in aligned LLMs. First, SCANS extracts the refusal steering vectors within the activation space and utilizes vocabulary projection to anchor some specific safety-critical layers which influence model refusal behavior. Second, by tracking the hidden state transition, SCANS identifies the steering direction and steers the model behavior accordingly, achieving a balance between exaggerated safety and adequate safety. Experiments show that SCANS achieves new state-of-the-art performance on XSTest and OKTest benchmarks, without impairing their defense capability against harmful queries and maintaining almost unchanged model capability.

papers.title: Understanding Refusal in Language Models with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How is refusal encoded in the latent space of LLMs, and how do adversarial jailbreaks suppress refusal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using sparse autoencoders to identify and causally validate refusal-related features in LLMs, revealing that harm and refusal are separately encoded and that adversarial jailbreaks suppress refusal features.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can identify causal refusal features, revealing the mediation of refusal by harmful features and the suppression mechanism of adversarial jailbreaks.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode harm and refusal as separate feature sets, with harmful features exhibiting a causal effect on refusal features.
Adversarial jailbreaks operate by suppressing specific refusal-related features.
The identified refusal features significantly improve classification on out-of-distribution adversarial examples.
The proposed CosSim+AP method identifies a minimal set of causal features for refusal behavior.
There is a conditional relationship where harmful features upstream trigger refusal features downstream.
papers.limitation:
The small K* may omit additional features relevant to harm and refusal.
The reliance on the refusal direction may not generalize to challenging instructions.
SAEs were trained on base models, not chat models, which may affect interpretability.
future_direction: Training SAEs on chat-model activations to improve feature interpretability and relevance.
papers.abstract: Refusal is a key safety behavior in aligned language models, yet the internal mechanisms driving refusals remain opaque. In this work, we conduct a mechanistic study of refusal in instruction-tuned LLMs using sparse autoencoders to identify latent features that causally mediate refusal behaviors. We apply our method to two open-source chat models and intervene on refusal-related features to assess their influence on generation, validating their behavioral impact across multiple harmful datasets. This enables a fine-grained inspection of how refusal manifests at the activation level and addresses key research questions such as investigating upstream-downstream latent relationship and understanding the mechanisms of adversarial jailbreaking techniques. We also establish the usefulness of refusal features in enhancing generalization for linear probes to out-of-distribution adversarial samples in classification tasks. We open source our code in https://github.com/wj210/refusal_sae.

papers.title: Energy-Driven Steering: Reducing False Refusals in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we reduce false refusals (over-refusal) in aligned large language models without compromising safety, using a fine-tuning free, inference-time intervention?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Energy Landscape Steering (ELS), a fine-tuning free framework that uses an externally trained Energy-Based Model to dynamically steer LLM hidden activations during inference, significantly reducing false refusals while maintaining safety and general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: ELS establishes a promising paradigm for building LLMs that simultaneously achieve high safety and low false refusal rates through inference-time activation steering.
papers.key_findings:
ELS raises compliance on the ORB-H false refusal benchmark from 57.3% to 82.6% for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct while maintaining baseline safety performance.
ELS outperforms existing fine-tuning free methods (Surgical, CAST, AdaSteer, AlphaSteer) in reducing false refusals without degrading safety or general knowledge.
ELS preserves general capabilities (MMLU, ARC-C, MATH accuracy) almost entirely, unlike fine-tuning methods which often degrade them.
ELS shows robustness against multi-turn jailbreak attacks, maintaining lower attack success rates compared to baselines.
The method is computationally efficient, adding minimal overhead during inference compared to other steering techniques.
papers.limitation:
ELS relies on an EBM trained on a fixed dataset, limiting its adaptability to emerging jailbreak tactics unseen during training.
Data labeling operates at the response level, not capturing partial compliance or mid-response refusal patterns, which could be beneficial for reasoning models.
future_direction: Make ELS an online method where the EBM continuously updates based on new interaction data.
Extend data labeling to a more fine-grained, sentence-level annotation scheme to capture partial compliance patterns.
Apply the method to reasoning models with chain-of-thought to rescue misaligned refusals during the thinking period.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) faces a key challenge: current alignment techniques often only focus on improving safety against harmful prompts, causing LLMs to become over-cautious and refuse to respond to benign prompts. Therefore, a key objective of safe alignment is to enhance safety while simultaneously reducing false refusals. In this paper, we introduce Energy-Driven Steering (EDS), a novel, fine-tuning free framework designed to resolve this challenge through dynamic, inference-time intervention. We trained a lightweight, external Energy-Based Model (EBM) to assign high energy to undesirable (false refusal or jailbreak) states and low energy to desirable (helpful response or safe reject) ones. During inference, EBM maps the LLM's internal activations to an "energy landscape". We use the gradient of the energy function to dynamically steer the LLM's hidden states to low energy regions, correcting the model to generate a desirable response in real-time without modifying its weights. This method decouples behavioral control from the model's core knowledge, offering a flexible solution with minimal computational overhead. Extensive experiments across a wide range of models show our method successfully achieves this objective: it substantially lowers false refusal rates. For example, raising compliance on the ORB-H benchmark from 57.3% to 82.6% while maintaining the baseline safety performance. Our work presents an effective paradigm for building LLMs that achieve both low false refusal rates and high safety.

papers.title: Safe-SAIL: Towards a Fine-grained Safety Landscape of Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoder Interpretation Framework
papers.research_question: Under what circumstances do sparse autoencoders (SAEs) derive the most fine-grained latent features for safety—a low-frequency concept domain? How can we efficiently identify SAEs with strong safety domain-specific interpretability and reduce the cost of feature explanation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Safe-SAIL, a framework for interpreting SAE features in safety-critical domains, which includes a pre-explanation evaluation metric to efficiently identify SAEs with strong safety domain-specific interpretability and reduces interpretation cost by 55% via segment-level simulation.
papers.conclusion: Safe-SAIL is a novel SAE interpretation framework that generates more granular safety feature explanations and reduces explanation costs by half, offering an internal perspective and methodology to address problems in LLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
Safe-SAIL reduces the cost of feature explanation by 55% through a segment-level simulation strategy while maintaining high correlation with token-level results.
The framework enables the identification of optimal SAE sparsity levels for safety domain-specific interpretability, which differs from the sparsity for minimal feature interference.
A comprehensive suite of SAEs trained on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct is released, with human-readable explanations for 1,758 safety-related features across pornography, politics, violence, and terror domains.
Empirical analyses reveal how LLMs encode specific real-world risk entities (e.g., pornographic websites) and safety-critical concepts across model layers.
The work provides insights into model cognition and reasoning trajectories, particularly highlighting failure modes in low-resource languages where relevant safety features are not activated.
papers.limitation:
The safety feature database covers only four major risk domains; extending it to emerging safety concerns would broaden applicability.
Explanation quality depends on the explainer model's capabilities, which may vary across languages and technical domains.
Segment-level simulation offers efficiency gains but approximates token-level dynamics; applications requiring maximal granularity may benefit from hybrid approaches.
Evaluation metrics rely on empirically validated thresholds that could benefit from automated domain-adaptive tuning.
Analyses primarily identify strong correlational patterns; establishing causal mechanisms through controlled interventions remains an important next step.
future_direction: Extending the safety feature database to emerging safety concerns such as privacy leakage, model self-replication, or deceptive alignment.
Improving explanation quality across languages and technical domains.
Developing hybrid simulation approaches for applications requiring maximal granularity.
Automated domain-adaptive tuning for evaluation metrics.
Systematic causal validation of the broader feature set through controlled interventions.
papers.abstract: Increasing deployment of large language models (LLMs) in real-world applications raises significant safety concerns. Most existing safety research focuses on evaluating LLM outputs or specific safety tasks, limiting their ability to address broader, undefined risks. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) facilitate interpretability research to clarify model behavior by explaining single-meaning atomic features decomposed from entangled signals. jHowever, prior applications on SAEs do not interpret features with fine-grained safety-related concepts, thus inadequately addressing safety-critical behaviors, such as generating toxic responses and violating safety regulations. For rigorous safety analysis, we must extract a rich and diverse set of safety-relevant features that effectively capture these high-risk behaviors, yet face two challenges: identifying SAEs with the greatest potential for generating safety concept-specific neurons, and the prohibitively high cost of detailed feature explanation. In this paper, we propose Safe-SAIL, a framework for interpreting SAE features within LLMs to advance mechanistic understanding in safety domains. Our approach systematically identifies SAE with best concept-specific interpretability, explains safety-related neurons, and introduces efficient strategies to scale up the interpretation process. We will release a comprehensive toolkit including SAE checkpoints and human-readable neuron explanations, which supports empirical analysis of safety risks to promote research on LLM safety.

papers.title: Hierarchical Safety Realignment: Lightweight Restoration of Safety in Pruned Large Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How to restore the safety performance of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) that degrades after network pruning?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a lightweight Hierarchical Safety Realignment (HSR) method that restores safety in pruned LVLMs by first identifying safety-critical attention heads and then restoring safety-critical neurons within those heads.
papers.conclusion: HSR effectively realigns the safety of pruned LVLMs through lightweight, hierarchical restoration of safety-critical neurons, facilitating the deployment of compact and reliable models.
papers.key_findings:
A small subset of neurons plays a disproportionately large role in ensuring model safety.
Some neurons negatively impact safety, and filtering them out improves safety realignment.
HSR can restore over 27% of lost safety in many cases with minimal neuron restoration (e.g., 0.020‱ of parameters).
The total Safety head importance score (Ships) strongly correlates with safety degradation after pruning.
HSR is also effective for Large Language Models (LLMs), not just LVLMs.
papers.limitation:
HSR may result in a slight loss of utility in certain cases.
HSR requires restoring a certain scale of neurons; there may be methods to restore safety at an even lower scale.
The safety recovery performance for LVLMs based on Llama3 is inferior to that of other models.
papers.abstract: With the increasing size of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), network pruning techniques aimed at compressing models for deployment in resource-constrained environments have garnered significant attention. However, we observe that pruning often leads to a degradation in safety performance. To address this issue, we present a novel and lightweight approach, termed Hierarchical Safety Realignment (HSR). HSR operates by first quantifying the contribution of each attention head to safety, identifying the most critical ones, and then selectively restoring neurons directly within these attention heads that play a pivotal role in maintaining safety. This process hierarchically realigns the safety of pruned LVLMs, progressing from the attention head level to the neuron level. We validate HSR across various models and pruning strategies, consistently achieving notable improvements in safety performance. To our knowledge, this is the first work explicitly focused on restoring safety in LVLMs post-pruning.

papers.title: Beyond I'm Sorry, I Can't: Dissecting Large Language Model Refusal
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms and causal features that govern refusal behavior in large language models when presented with harmful prompts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a pipeline combining sparse autoencoders and factorization machines to isolate causal features for LLM refusal, revealing redundant 'hydra' features that activate when others are suppressed.
papers.conclusion: Presents a pipeline for isolating causal refusal features using SAEs and factorization machines, revealing feature redundancy and interactions, laying groundwork for feature-level steering of refusal behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating specific SAE features can jailbreak models, flipping refusal to compliance on harmful prompts.
Redundant features exist that remain dormant until other features are ablated, demonstrating a hydra effect in refusal mechanisms.
Factorization machines capture non-linear feature interactions better than linear probes for identifying jailbreak-critical features.
Jailbreak-critical features can be mapped to harm categories in an unsafe taxonomy, though with limited human alignment.
The refusal mechanism involves non-linear interactions among features, as shown by the superior performance of factorization machines over linear probes.
papers.limitation:
