The proposed activation editing method, which applies small, distributed shifts to neuron activations based on their alignment to a toxicity representation, outperforms DPO in reducing toxicity while preserving perplexity, without requiring weight updates.
papers.limitation:
Using a linear probe captures toxicity as a single direction, but toxicity may be better represented as a subspace capturing different aspects (e.g., hate speech, abusive language).
The projection method assumes neurons contribute proportionally along their activated directions, but toxicity representations may be distributed across more complex linear combinations of neurons.
The four neuron groups and activation editing method are demonstrated for toxicity reduction; generalizing them to other binary safety tasks (e.g., bias, misinformation) or to general instruction-tuned models requires future work.
future_direction: More robust analysis of toxic subspace projections instead of a single direction.
Extending the four neuron groups analysis to other binary safety-related tasks trained with DPO (e.g., biased vs. unbiased content).
Extending the activation editing method to other safety-related tasks or general tasks where a linear concept representation can be derived.
papers.abstract: Safety fine-tuning algorithms reduce harmful outputs in language models, yet their mechanisms remain under-explored. Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a popular choice of algorithm, but prior explanations, attributing its effects solely to dampened toxic neurons in the MLP layers, are incomplete. In this study, we analyse four language models (Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-2B, Mistral-7B, GPT-2-Medium) and show that toxic neurons only account for 2.5% to 24% of DPO's effects across models. Instead, DPO balances distributed activation shifts across all MLP neurons to create a net toxicity reduction. We attribute this reduction to four neuron groups, two aligned with reducing toxicity and two promoting anti-toxicity, whose combined effects replicate DPO across models. To further validate this understanding, we develop an activation editing method mimicking DPO through distributed shifts along a toxicity representation. This method outperforms DPO in reducing toxicity while preserving perplexity, without requiring any weight updates. Our work provides a mechanistic understanding of DPO and introduces an efficient, tuning-free alternative for safety fine-tuning.

papers.title: Preemptive Detection and Steering of LLM Misalignment via Latent Reachability
papers.research_question: How can reachability analysis be used for preemptive detection and steering of LLM misalignment at inference time?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces BRT-ALIGN, a reachability-based framework for preemptive detection and steering of LLM misalignment at inference time by modeling generation as a dynamical system in latent space and learning a safety value function.
papers.conclusion: Reachability analysis provides a principled and practical foundation for inference-time LLM safety, enabling preemptive detection and steering of unsafe trajectories.
papers.key_findings:
BRT-ALIGN provides accurate and early detection of unsafe completions, flagging them 7-10 tokens in advance.
BRT-ALIGN steers LLM responses to be safer (higher safety rate) while preserving sentence diversity and with only a moderate coherence trade-off.
BRT-ALIGN outperforms baselines (SAP and RE-CONTROL) in runtime monitoring (F1 score) and alignment (safety rate) across multiple LLMs and datasets.
BRT-ALIGN reduces unsafe generations and can make models less violent, profane, offensive, and politically biased, as shown in qualitative examples.
BRT-ALIGN has lower inference time overhead compared to gradient-based baselines.
papers.limitation:
Relies on an offensive language classifier, which may not cover all forms of harm (e.g., misinformation, self-harm encouragement).
For some models (e.g., Ministral-8B-Instruct-2410), BRT-ALIGN exhibits reduced semantic coherence compared to other methods.
Evaluation is limited to offensive responses in open-source models; real-world, high-stakes settings require broader assessment.
future_direction: Extend the framework to richer, multi-dimensional notions of harm beyond offensive language.
Explore more advanced control-theoretic strategies (e.g., smooth blending filters, control barrier functions) to mitigate coherence trade-offs.
Apply BRT-ALIGN in real-world, high-stakes settings (e.g., medical, legal, educational LLMs) with broader datasets and robustness assessments.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now ubiquitous in everyday tools, raising urgent safety concerns about their tendency to generate harmful content. The dominant safety approach -- reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) -- effectively shapes model behavior during training but offers no safeguards at inference time, where unsafe continuations may still arise. We propose BRT-Align, a reachability-based framework that brings control-theoretic safety tools to LLM inference. BRT-Align models autoregressive generation as a dynamical system in latent space and learn a safety value function via backward reachability, estimating the worst-case evolution of a trajectory. This enables two complementary mechanisms: (1) a runtime monitor that forecasts unsafe completions several tokens in advance, and (2) a least-restrictive steering filter that minimally perturbs latent states to redirect generation away from unsafe regions. Experiments across multiple LLMs and toxicity benchmarks demonstrate that BRT-Align provides more accurate and earlier detection of unsafe continuations than baselines. Moreover, for LLM safety alignment, BRT-Align substantially reduces unsafe generations while preserving sentence diversity and coherence. Qualitative results further highlight emergent alignment properties: BRT-Align consistently produces responses that are less violent, less profane, less offensive, and less politically biased. Together, these findings demonstrate that reachability analysis provides a principled and practical foundation for inference-time LLM safety.

papers.title: On the Role of Attention Heads in Large Language Model Safety
papers.research_question: What is the connection between standard attention mechanisms and safety capability in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Ships and Sahara to identify safety-critical attention heads in LLMs, showing that ablating a small number of these heads significantly reduces model safety.
papers.conclusion: Ships and Sahara provide a novel perspective for interpreting safety in LLMs, revealing that specific attention heads are crucial for safety and are sparsely distributed.
papers.key_findings:
Safety attention heads are sparse; ablating them significantly increases the attack success rate (ASR).
Safety heads primarily function as feature extractors for safety.
Models fine-tuned from the same base model exhibit overlapping safety heads.
Ablating safety heads has minimal impact on model helpfulness.
The proposed method localizes safety parameters at a finer granularity (head-level) compared to prior work.
future_direction: Exploring the association between attention heads and other safety capabilities beyond direct rejection.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve state-of-the-art performance on multiple language tasks, yet their safety guardrails can be circumvented, leading to harmful generations. In light of this, recent research on safety mechanisms has emerged, revealing that when safety representations or component are suppressed, the safety capability of LLMs are compromised. However, existing research tends to overlook the safety impact of multi-head attention mechanisms, despite their crucial role in various model functionalities. Hence, in this paper, we aim to explore the connection between standard attention mechanisms and safety capability to fill this gap in the safety-related mechanistic interpretability. We propose a novel metric which tailored for multi-head attention, the Safety Head ImPortant Score (Ships), to assess the individual heads' contributions to model safety. Based on this, we generalize Ships to the dataset level and further introduce the Safety Attention Head AttRibution Algorithm (Sahara) to attribute the critical safety attention heads inside the model. Our findings show that the special attention head has a significant impact on safety. Ablating a single safety head allows aligned model (e.g., Llama-2-7b-chat) to respond to 16 times more harmful queries, while only modifying 0.006% of the parameters, in contrast to the ~ 5% modification required in previous studies. More importantly, we demonstrate that attention heads primarily function as feature extractors for safety and models fine-tuned from the same base model exhibit overlapping safety heads through comprehensive experiments. Together, our attribution approach and findings provide a novel perspective for unpacking the black box of safety mechanisms within large models.

papers.title: Towards Understanding and Improving Refusal in Compressed Models via Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How does the refusal mechanism change in compressed models, and why are quantized models safer than pruned ones? Additionally, how can we improve the safety of compressed models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that compressed models retain a single-direction refusal mechanism, but pruning alters this direction leading to safety loss, and introduces AIRD to improve safety of compressed models without performance degradation.
papers.conclusion: The refusal mechanism changes in pruned models, explaining safety loss, and AIRD can effectively improve safety without harming performance.
papers.key_findings:
The refusal mechanism is still mediated by a single direction in compressed models.
In pruned models, the source position of the refusal direction changes, while in quantized models it remains the same.
The change in refusal direction correlates with loss of safety in pruned models.
Quantized models are safer than pruned models because they retain the original refusal direction.
AIRD can improve safety of pruned models without significant performance loss.
papers.limitation:
Findings may not generalize to non-transformer architectures like Mixture of Experts, State Space Models, and RNNs.
AIRD reduces the compression rate by decreasing sparsity in one layer.
future_direction: Generalize findings to non-transformer architectures.
Optimize AIRD to mitigate compression rate reduction.
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of large language models has spurred significant interest in model compression as a means to enhance their accessibility and practicality. While extensive research has explored model compression through the lens of safety, findings suggest that safety-aligned models often lose elements of trustworthiness post-compression. Simultaneously, the field of mechanistic interpretability has gained traction, with notable discoveries, such as the identification of a single direction in the residual stream mediating refusal behaviors across diverse model architectures. In this work, we investigate the safety of compressed models by examining the mechanisms of refusal, adopting a novel interpretability-driven perspective to evaluate model safety. Furthermore, leveraging insights from our interpretability analysis, we propose a lightweight, computationally efficient method to enhance the safety of compressed models without compromising their performance or utility.

papers.title: The Hidden Space of Safety: Understanding Preference-Tuned LLMs in Multilingual context
papers.research_question: How does alignment (preference tuning) affect the hidden representations of LLMs across different languages, and does it generalize effectively beyond English?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that alignment induces a separation between safe and unsafe representations in the hidden space for English, but this effect is significantly weaker for other languages, highlighting a monolingual bias in current preference-tuning methods.
papers.conclusion: State-of-the-art preference-tuned models exhibit a monolingual bias, with alignment being effective in English but inconsistent across other languages, underscoring the need for language-specific fine-tuning to ensure robust multilingual safety.
papers.key_findings:
Alignment improves cluster separation between harmful and harmless prompts in English but shows inconsistent and weaker effects in Hindi, Chinese, and German.
Quantitative metrics (Bhattacharyya Distance, Silhouette Score) confirm stronger alignment-induced separation in English compared to other languages.
In a parallel text-detoxification setting, alignment fails to induce a clear distribution shift for Hindi, indicating language-dependent representation learning.
The study finds that some models (e.g., for Hindi) can show greater cluster separation in the unaligned reference model than in the aligned model, indicating potential alignment degradation.
Current alignment strategies, optimized on English-centric preference data, do not generalize robustly to multilingual settings, leading to safety inconsistencies.
papers.limitation:
The study primarily focuses on safety alignment, overlooking other critical domains such as multi-modality, reasoning, instruction-following, or planning due to the lack of standardized multilingual benchmarks for these tasks.
Only three non-English languages (Hindi, Chinese, German), all medium-resource, are evaluated, limiting generalizability to low-resource languages.
The dataset consists of 5,000 sentences, which may not fully capture the diversity of real-world multilingual scenarios.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to low-resource languages to better understand alignment disparities.
Use a broader dataset to further validate findings across different linguistic and cultural contexts.
Prioritize multilingual preference collection and explore synthetic techniques to transfer alignment knowledge from English to other languages.
papers.abstract: Alignment tuning has enabled large language models to excel in reasoning, instruction-following, and minimizing harmful generations. However, despite their widespread deployment, these models exhibit a monolingual bias, raising concerns about the effectiveness of alignment across languages. Current alignment methods predominantly focus on English, leaving it unclear how alignment mechanism generalize to multilingual settings. To address this, we conduct a systematic analysis of distributional shifts in the embedding space of LLMs before and after alignment, uncovering its impact on model behavior across diverse languages. We leverage the alignment-induced separation in safety space as a quantitative tool to measure how alignment enforces safety constraints. Our study evaluates seven LLMs using balanced toxicity datasets and parallel text-detoxification benchmarks, revealing substantial disparities in the latent representation space between high-resource and low-resource languages. These findings underscore the need for language-specific fine-tuning to ensure fair, reliable and robust multilingual alignment. Our insights provide a foundation for developing truly safe multilingual LLMs, emphasizing the urgency of addressing alignment gaps in underrepresented languages.

papers.title: How Alignment and Jailbreak Work: Explain LLM Safety through Intermediate Hidden States
papers.research_question: How do alignment and jailbreak work in large language models? The paper investigates the mechanisms of safety alignment and how jailbreak circumvents it by analyzing intermediate hidden states.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs learn ethical concepts during pre-training and can identify malicious inputs in early layers. Safety alignment associates these early concepts with positive/negative emotions in middle layers, which are refined into accept/reject tokens. Jailbreak works by disturbing this association.
papers.conclusion: The work explains how alignment and jailbreak function through intermediate hidden states, enhancing transparency and offering a new perspective for LLM safety development.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs learn ethical concepts during pre-training, not just from alignment.
Weak classifiers can distinguish malicious and normal inputs from early layer hidden states with >95% accuracy.
Alignment associates early ethical concepts with emotion guesses (positive/negative) in middle layers, which are refined into stylistic accept/reject tokens.
Jailbreak does not deceive early ethical classification but disturbs the association between early and middle layers.
Logit Grafting, which grafts positive emotions onto malicious inputs, approximates jailbreak and confirms the disturbance mechanism.
papers.limitation: Used default settings of simple weak classifiers and only examined safety perspective; method might generalize to other capabilities but not tested.
future_direction: Apply the method to interpret other capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) rely on safety alignment to avoid responding to malicious user inputs. Unfortunately, jailbreak can circumvent safety guardrails, resulting in LLMs generating harmful content and raising concerns about LLM safety. Due to language models with intensive parameters often regarded as black boxes, the mechanisms of alignment and jailbreak are challenging to elucidate. In this paper, we employ weak classifiers to explain LLM safety through the intermediate hidden states. We first confirm that LLMs learn ethical concepts during pre-training rather than alignment and can identify malicious and normal inputs in the early layers. Alignment actually associates the early concepts with emotion guesses in the middle layers and then refines them to the specific reject tokens for safe generations. Jailbreak disturbs the transformation of early unethical classification into negative emotions. We conduct experiments on models from 7B to 70B across various model families to prove our conclusion. Overall, our paper indicates the intrinsical mechanism of LLM safety and how jailbreaks circumvent safety guardrails, offering a new perspective on LLM safety and reducing concerns. Our code is available at https://github.com/ydyjya/LLM-IHS-Explanation.

papers.title: SafeInfer: Context Adaptive Decoding Time Safety Alignment for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we improve the safety alignment of large language models at decoding time to reduce harmful responses while preserving utility?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAFE INFER, a two-phase decoding-time safety alignment strategy that combines safety amplification (adjusting hidden states with safe demonstrations) and safety-guided decoding (influencing token selection) to reduce harmful responses while preserving model utility.
papers.conclusion: SAFE INFER is an effective decoding-time safety alignment strategy that significantly reduces harmful responses across various models, datasets, and prompting techniques while maintaining the model's general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
SAFE INFER achieves the lowest attack success rates (ASR) across multiple safety datasets (e.g., 1.09% on HarmEval for Llama-2) compared to baselines like SafeDecoding and Self-CD.
The method is effective against various jailbreak attacks (GCG, AutoDAN, PAIR, DeepInception, GPTFuzzer), reducing ASR to near zero in some cases.
SAFE INFER preserves the utility of base models on benchmarks like MMLU and TruthfulQA, with minimal performance drop.
The method also works on edited models (using ROME), significantly reducing the increased harmfulness introduced by model editing.
SAFE INFER shows effectiveness across different prompting techniques: simple, instruction-centric, and instruction-centric chain-of-thought prompts.
papers.abstract: Safety-aligned language models often exhibit fragile and imbalanced safety mechanisms, increasing the likelihood of generating unsafe content. In addition, incorporating new knowledge through editing techniques to language models can further compromise safety. To address these issues, we propose SafeInfer, a context-adaptive, decoding-time safety alignment strategy for generating safe responses to user queries. SafeInfer comprises two phases: the safety amplification phase, which employs safe demonstration examples to adjust the model's hidden states and increase the likelihood of safer outputs, and the safety-guided decoding phase, which influences token selection based on safety-optimized distributions, ensuring the generated content complies with ethical guidelines. Further, we present HarmEval, a novel benchmark for extensive safety evaluations, designed to address potential misuse scenarios in accordance with the policies of leading AI tech giants.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: Alignment Via Interpretability: Layerwise Counterfactuals To Detect Maladaptive Llm Behaviors
papers.research_question: How can layerwise counterfactual interventions on internal representations detect maladaptive behaviors in large language models that are not reliably exposed through prompt-based evaluation alone?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a layerwise counterfactual interpretability framework that detects maladaptive behaviors in LLMs by performing causal interventions on internal representations, demonstrating that intermediate layers encode decision-critical features for alignment.
papers.conclusion: The layerwise counterfactual framework enables proactive detection of alignment risks by revealing internal representations causally linked to maladaptive behaviors, positioning interpretability as a diagnostic tool for safety.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers consistently show the highest causal influence on alignment behavior, often flipping responses between refusal and compliance.
Counterfactual interventions can induce maladaptive behaviors even when baseline outputs appear aligned, revealing latent misalignment.
Layerwise sensitivity patterns are stable across different model checkpoints and random seeds.
Early layers encode surface linguistic features with minimal impact on alignment decisions.
Late layers modulate stylistic aspects of responses rather than core decision outcomes.
papers.limitation:
Counterfactual interventions establish causal influence but do not directly reveal how misalignment features are learned during training.
The analysis focuses on decoder-only transformer architectures, and findings may not fully generalize to other model families or multimodal systems.
Behavioral evaluation metrics, though carefully designed, cannot exhaustively capture all forms of maladaptive behavior.
Interpretability methods may miss distributed or nonlinear representations that do not localize cleanly within individual layers.
future_direction: Extending the framework to larger models, multimodal architectures, and training time interventions.
Integrating counterfactual diagnostics into alignment training loops.
Formalizing metrics for internal alignment robustness.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Large language model alignment remains fragile under distribution shift, jailbreak prompts, and latent goal misgeneralization, motivating the need for diagnostic tools that move beyond surface level behavior to internal representations. This paper investigates alignment via interpretability by introducing a layerwise counterfactual analysis framework that probes how targeted interventions on hidden states alter downstream model behavior. Using publicly available transformer based language models and open interpretability tooling, we perform controlled counterfactual substitutions and activation patching across layers to detect maladaptive behaviors that are not reliably exposed through prompt based evaluation alone. Our analysis demonstrates that specific intermediate layers encode decision critical features whose perturbation consistently induces alignment failures such as reward hacking tendencies, deceptive compliance, and instruction misgeneralization, even when input level behavior appears aligned. We further show that these internal signatures are stable across random seeds and model checkpoints, enabling reproducible detection of misalignment risks prior to deployment. The findings support the thesis that interpretability driven diagnostics can serve as an early warning mechanism for alignment failures and provide a principled foundation for integrating internal model transparency into safety evaluation pipelines.

papers.title: SAFEx: Analyzing Vulnerabilities of MoE-Based LLMs via Stable Safety-critical Expert Identification
papers.research_question: How does the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture in large language models introduce a positional vulnerability where safety-aligned behaviors rely on specific expert modules, and how can this vulnerability be systematically analyzed and mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAFEX, an analytical framework to identify and validate safety-critical experts in MoE-based LLMs, formalizing and demonstrating the positional vulnerability where safety alignment disproportionately depends on a small set of experts.
papers.conclusion: The work establishes positional vulnerability as a distinct MoE-specific safety challenge and provides a practical, compute-efficient pathway for expert-level safety interventions within routed architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Safety-aligned behavior in MoE models is highly concentrated in a small number of experts; masking 12 selected experts in Qwen3-30B-A3B reduces the refusal rate by 22%.
Jailbreak attacks cause a significant shift in expert activation patterns, exploiting the positional vulnerability and leading to unsafe outputs.
Lightweight LoRA adaptation targeted at identified safety-critical expert groups (HRCG and HCDG) can improve refusal rates under adversarial prompts without full-model retraining.
MoE-based models exhibit greater susceptibility to jailbreak attacks compared to their dense counterparts, highlighting an architectural vulnerability.
future_direction: Developing more robust alignment algorithms specifically designed for MoE-based language models.
Research on safety-enhanced MoE architectures.
papers.abstract: Large language models with Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures achieve efficiency and scalability, yet their routing mechanisms introduce safety alignment challenges insufficiently addressed by techniques developed for dense models. In this work, the MoE-specific safety risk of positional vulnerability-that safety-aligned behaviors rely on specific expert modules-is formalized and systematically analyzed. An analytical framework, SAFEx, is presented to robustly identify, characterize, and validate safety-critical experts via a stability-based expert selection procedure, and to decompose them into two functional groups: the Harmful Content Detection Group (HCDG), which specializes in identifying and recognizing harmful content within user inputs, and the Harmful Response Control Group (HRCG), which specializes in controlling and enforcing model behaviors to generate appropriate safety responses. Expert-level interventions are conducted to probe causality and to test mitigation. Targeted masking of SAFEx-selected experts reveals that safety behavior is highly concentrated. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, configured with 48 MoE-FFN layers and 128 experts per layer under top-8 routing (48x128=6,144 experts in total), disabling 12 selected experts reduces the refusal rate by 22%. In addition, lightweight adaptation is performed using LoRA under three configurations-the HRCG, the union of HCDG and HRCG, and all experts-and the resulting updates are composed through negative weight merging targeted at the HRCG, leading to improved refusal under adversarial prompts without full-model retraining. These results establish positional vulnerability as a distinct MoE-specific safety challenge and provide a practical, compute-efficient pathway for expert-level safety interventions within routed architectures.

papers.title: SafeSteer: Interpretable Safety Steering with Refusal-Evasion in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we steer large language model outputs for safety at inference time without fine-tuning, using activation steering with category-specific vectors?
papers.core_contribution: SAFE STEER enables precise, customizable safety adjustments in LLMs through category-specific steering vectors computed from activations, without fine-tuning or contrastive data, while maintaining text quality.
papers.conclusion: SAFE STEER demonstrates effective inference-time safety steering across LLMs and datasets, providing precise control, preventing blanket refusals, and guiding models to generate safe, contextually relevant content.
papers.key_findings:
SAFE STEER reduces the percentage of unsafe responses in LLMs across various harm categories.
It effectively uses generic safe data without requiring contrastive paired datasets.
Pruning activations based on L2 norms improves steering signals and safety outcomes.
The method outperforms baselines like SEA and CAA in safety and utility metrics.
Steering maintains or improves text quality attributes such as helpfulness and coherence while enhancing safety.
future_direction: Investigate transferability of steering vectors across models and categories.
Scale up the method to more harm categories and models for broader applicability.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) to adapt to evolving safety policies is costly and impractical. Mechanistic interpretability enables inference-time control through latent activation steering, yet its potential for precise, customizable safety adjustments remains largely untapped. This paper investigates an approach called SafeSteer for guiding the outputs of LLMs by: (i) leveraging category-specific steering vectors for more precise control, (ii) employing a simple, gradient-free unsupervised method to enhance safety steering while preserving text quality, topic relevance, and without explicit refusal, and (iii) accomplishing this without a hard requirement of contrastive pairwise safe data. We also highlight that our method, being simple and effective, aligns with recent studies suggesting that simple techniques often outperform more complex ones in activation steering. We showcase the effectiveness of our approach across various LLMs, datasets, and risk categories, demonstrating its ability to provide precise control, prevent blanket refusals, and guide models toward generating safe content while maintaining topic relevance.

papers.title: NeuroBreak: Unveil Internal Jailbreak Mechanisms in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do jailbreak attacks exploit internal mechanisms in large language models to bypass safety alignments?
papers.core_contribution: NeuroBreak is a visual analytics system that unveils internal jailbreak mechanisms in LLMs by analyzing neuron-level safety mechanisms and enabling targeted fine-tuning to mitigate vulnerabilities.
papers.conclusion: NeuroBreak enhances expert understanding of LLM security mechanisms and supports precise alignment efforts through visual analysis and targeted fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
NeuroBreak enables progressive exploration from macroscopic behavior to neuron-level mechanisms in jailbreak attacks.
It identifies safety neurons and categorizes them into functional archetypes based on toxicity vectors and activation patterns.
The system reveals that layers 15-28 encode discriminative harmful features with high probe accuracy.
Targeted fine-tuning of safety neurons using NeuroBreak improves model robustness against jailbreak attacks.
NeuroBreak provides visual evidence for neuron cooperation patterns and vulnerabilities in LLM safety mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on linear probing may miss nonlinear semantic shifts influencing adversarial behaviors.
Lack of dynamic adversarial interactions or real-time adaptation to evolving threats.
future_direction: Explore nonlinear probing techniques for more complex decision boundaries.
Incorporate dynamic adversarial training or online learning for real-time adaptation.
papers.abstract: In deployment and application, large language models (LLMs) typically undergo safety alignment to prevent illegal and unethical outputs. However, the continuous advancement of jailbreak attack techniques, designed to bypass safety mechanisms with adversarial prompts, has placed increasing pressure on the security defenses of LLMs. Strengthening resistance to jailbreak attacks requires an in-depth understanding of the security mechanisms and vulnerabilities of LLMs. However, the vast number of parameters and complex structure of LLMs make analyzing security weaknesses from an internal perspective a challenging task. This paper presents NeuroBreak, a top-down jailbreak analysis system designed to analyze neuron-level safety mechanisms and mitigate vulnerabilities. We carefully design system requirements through collaboration with three experts in the field of AI security. The system provides a comprehensive analysis of various jailbreak attack methods. By incorporating layer-wise representation probing analysis, NeuroBreak offers a novel perspective on the model's decision-making process throughout its generation steps. Furthermore, the system supports the analysis of critical neurons from both semantic and functional perspectives, facilitating a deeper exploration of security mechanisms. We conduct quantitative evaluations and case studies to verify the effectiveness of our system, offering mechanistic insights for developing next-generation defense strategies against evolving jailbreak attacks.

papers.title: VLM-Guard: Safeguarding Vision-Language Models via Fulfilling Safety Alignment Gap
papers.research_question: How can vision-language models (VLMs) be safeguarded from harmful queries and jailbreak attacks by addressing the safety alignment gap caused by the modality gap?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes VLM-GUARD, an inference-time intervention that leverages the safety-aligned LLM component of a VLM to supervise safety alignment by projecting VLM representations into a subspace orthogonal to a safety steering direction extracted from the LLM.
papers.conclusion: VLM-GUARD effectively reduces the attack success rate of VLMs against harmful instructions and jailbreak attacks by fulfilling the safety alignment gap.
papers.key_findings:
VLM-GUARD outperforms baseline methods (Self-Reminder and Goal Priority) in reducing attack success rate across three malicious query settings.
VLM-GUARD narrows the safety alignment gap between the VLM and its LLM component, maintaining a clear distinction between harmful and harmless queries even with visual input.
The method does not compromise the quality and fluency of model responses, as indicated by low perplexity scores.
papers.limitation:
The approach primarily intervenes at the inference stage and does not address the issue comprehensively during the training phase.
While the work explores the impact of the modality gap on VLM safety, its influence on other capabilities such as reasoning and understanding remains to be investigated.
The visual validation of the modality gap's impact on safety used a simple blank image, though the influence persists with normal images.
papers.abstract: The emergence of vision language models (VLMs) comes with increased safety concerns, as the incorporation of multiple modalities heightens vulnerability to attacks. Although VLMs can be built upon LLMs that have textual safety alignment, it is easily undermined when the vision modality is integrated. We attribute this safety challenge to the modality gap, a separation of image and text in the shared representation space, which blurs the distinction between harmful and harmless queries that is evident in LLMs but weakened in VLMs. To avoid safety decay and fulfill the safety alignment gap, we propose VLM-Guard, an inference-time intervention strategy that leverages the LLM component of a VLM as supervision for the safety alignment of the VLM. VLM-Guard projects the representations of VLM into the subspace that is orthogonal to the safety steering direction that is extracted from the safety-aligned LLM. Experimental results on three malicious instruction settings show the effectiveness of VLM-Guard in safeguarding VLM and fulfilling the safety alignment gap between VLM and its LLM component.

papers.title: Persona Features Control Emergent Misalignment
papers.research_question: When, why, and how does fine-tuning language models on narrow incorrect datasets lead to broad, undesirable misalignment (emergent misalignment), and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Emergent misalignment occurs across diverse fine-tuning and reinforcement learning settings and is mediated by 'misaligned persona' features in activation space, which can be used to detect, steer, and mitigate the behavior.
papers.conclusion: Emergent misalignment is a robust phenomenon that can arise from various training procedures, and interpretability methods like model-diffing with sparse autoencoders can reveal its mechanistic basis and enable detection and mitigation strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Emergent misalignment occurs from supervised fine-tuning on narrow incorrect advice in diverse domains and from reinforcement learning that rewards incorrect responses.
A 'toxic persona' feature (and other related features) identified via sparse autoencoder model-diffing causally controls emergent misalignment and can be used to steer model behavior.
Fine-tuning an emergently misaligned model on a few hundred benign samples efficiently re-aligns the model.
The activation level of the 'toxic persona' feature can discriminate between aligned and misaligned models, serving as a potential early-warning signal.
Emergent misalignment generally increases with model size for models capable of coherent responses.
papers.limitation: Fine-tuning on natural human-generated data produces high incoherence and correlated misalignment, which may be a different effect from the emergent misalignment observed with synthetic data.
future_direction: Further work to understand training dynamics, especially the effects of off-policy fine-tuning on human data.
papers.abstract: Understanding how language models generalize behaviors from their training to a broader deployment distribution is an important problem in AI safety. Betley et al. discovered that fine-tuning GPT-4o on intentionally insecure code causes "emergent misalignment," where models give stereotypically malicious responses to unrelated prompts. We extend this work, demonstrating emergent misalignment across diverse conditions, including reinforcement learning on reasoning models, fine-tuning on various synthetic datasets, and in models without safety training. To investigate the mechanisms behind this generalized misalignment, we apply a "model diffing" approach using sparse autoencoders to compare internal model representations before and after fine-tuning. This approach reveals several "misaligned persona" features in activation space, including a toxic persona feature which most strongly controls emergent misalignment and can be used to predict whether a model will exhibit such behavior. Additionally, we investigate mitigation strategies, discovering that fine-tuning an emergently misaligned model on just a few hundred benign samples efficiently restores alignment.

papers.title: ASGuard: Activation-Scaling Guard to Mitigate Targeted Jailbreaking Attack
papers.research_question: How can we surgically mitigate targeted jailbreaking vulnerabilities in LLMs by understanding and intervening in their internal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ASGUARD, a framework that uses circuit analysis to identify vulnerable attention heads and then applies activation scaling and preventative fine-tuning to mitigate targeted jailbreaking attacks while preserving model utility.
papers.conclusion: ASGUARD demonstrates how mechanistic interpretability can be leveraged to develop targeted and efficient safety interventions, achieving a superior safety-utility trade-off.
papers.key_findings:
Tense jailbreaking is mediated by specific attention heads that can be identified via circuit analysis.
ASGUARD reduces the attack success rate of tense jailbreaking from 42% to 8% in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct while maintaining high utility.
ASGUARD achieves a Pareto-optimal balance between safety and utility, outperforming baseline methods like SFT and DPO.
The method generalizes to other jailbreaking attacks like GCG and LogiBreak.
Preventative fine-tuning helps the model learn a robust refusal mechanism without relying on the vulnerable pathway.
papers.limitation:
The method requires constructing circuits for each specific attack type, which can be computationally expensive.
There is a risk of over-refusal if the scaling vectors are not properly tuned.
future_direction: Extending ASGUARD to other types of jailbreaking attacks and models.
Automating the circuit discovery process to reduce computational cost.
Exploring the application of activation scaling to other safety vulnerabilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs), despite being safety-aligned, exhibit brittle refusal behaviors that can be circumvented by simple linguistic changes. As tense jailbreaking demonstrates that models refusing harmful requests often comply when rephrased in past tense, a critical generalization gap is revealed in current alignment methods whose underlying mechanisms are poorly understood. In this work, we introduce Activation-Scaling Guard (ASGuard), an insightful, mechanistically-informed framework that surgically mitigates this specific vulnerability. For the first step, we use circuit analysis to identify the specific attention heads causally linked to the targeted jailbreaking, the tense-changing attack. Second, we train a precise, channel-wise scaling vector to recalibrate the activation of tense vulnerable heads. Lastly, we apply it into a "preventative fine-tuning", forcing the model to learn a more robust refusal mechanism. Across three LLMs, ASGuard effectively reduces the attack success rate of targeted jailbreaking while preserving general capabilities and minimizing over refusal, achieving a Pareto-optimal balance between safety and utility. Our findings underscore how adversarial suffixes suppress the propagation of the refusal-mediating direction, based on mechanistic analysis. Furthermore, our work showcases how a deep understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical, efficient, and targeted methods for adjusting model behavior, charting a course for more reliable and interpretable AI safety.

papers.title: LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately
papers.research_question: Do LLMs encode harmfulness and refusal as separate concepts internally, and how can this separation be analyzed?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode harmfulness and refusal separately in their internal representations, and the harmfulness direction extracted at the instruction token can be used to manipulate and analyze model safety.
papers.conclusion: LLMs encode harmfulness and refusal separately, providing a new dimension for understanding and improving AI safety mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Harmfulness is encoded at the last token of the user instruction (t_inst), while refusal is encoded at the last token of the post-instruction tokens (t_post-inst).
Steering along the harmfulness direction can cause LLMs to reinterpret harmless inputs as harmful, while steering along the refusal direction only reinforces refusal behavior without changing harmfulness judgment.
Jailbreak methods often work by suppressing refusal signals without altering the model's internal belief that the instruction is harmful.
Harmfulness representations are fine-grained and vary across risk categories, whereas refusal directions are similar across categories.
The latent harmfulness representation can be used to build an intrinsic safeguard (Latent Guard) that performs comparably to finetuned safety models.
papers.limitation:
The study does not investigate the role of different layers in formulating refusal and harmfulness.
Experiments are limited to 7B and 8B models, so findings may not generalize to larger models.
future_direction: Study the role of each layer in harmfulness and refusal representations.
Investigate how harmfulness and refusal encoding changes with model size.
Use circuit analysis to understand the relation between internal harmfulness belief and external refusal behavior.
papers.abstract: LLMs are trained to refuse harmful instructions, but do they truly understand harmfulness beyond just refusing? Prior work has shown that LLMs' refusal behaviors can be mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, i.e., a refusal direction. In this work, we identify a new dimension to analyze safety mechanisms in LLMs, i.e., harmfulness, which is encoded internally as a separate concept from refusal. There exists a harmfulness direction that is distinct from the refusal direction. As causal evidence, steering along the harmfulness direction can lead LLMs to interpret harmless instructions as harmful, but steering along the refusal direction tends to elicit refusal responses directly without reversing the model's judgment on harmfulness. Furthermore, using our identified harmfulness concept, we find that certain jailbreak methods work by reducing the refusal signals without reversing the model's internal belief of harmfulness. We also find that adversarially finetuning models to accept harmful instructions has minimal impact on the model's internal belief of harmfulness. These insights lead to a practical safety application: The model's latent harmfulness representation can serve as an intrinsic safeguard (Latent Guard) for detecting unsafe inputs and reducing over-refusals that is robust to finetuning attacks. For instance, our Latent Guard achieves performance comparable to or better than Llama Guard 3 8B, a dedicated finetuned safeguard model, across different jailbreak methods. Our findings suggest that LLMs' internal understanding of harmfulness is more robust than their refusal decision to diverse input instructions, offering a new perspective to study AI safety.

papers.title: JailbreakLens: Interpreting Jailbreak Mechanism in the Lens of Representation and Circuit
papers.research_question: How do jailbreak prompts affect the internal representations of LLMs? Which model components are critical to generation safety? How do internal representations and key model components evolve throughout the token generation process during jailbreak attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes JailbreakLens, a dual-perspective interpretation framework that analyzes jailbreak mechanisms by examining representation shifts and circuit activations, revealing how jailbreak prompts deceive LLMs by manipulating harmfulness perception and safety-critical components.
papers.conclusion: JailbreakLens provides insights into jailbreak mechanisms, showing that prompts deceive models by shifting representations and manipulating key circuits, with a consistent correlation between representation deception and circuit activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak prompts deceive LLMs by shifting their internal representations towards safe clusters, making harmful prompts appear safe.
Key circuits, such as specific attention heads and MLP layers, are manipulated to suppress refusal behaviors and encourage affirmation.
There is a strong correlation between representation deception and activation shifts in key circuits across diverse jailbreak methods and LLMs.
Rule-based and demonstration-based jailbreak methods are more deceptive than gradient-based or evolutionary-based methods.
Dynamic analysis shows that jailbreak effects evolve during token generation, with refusal signals sometimes initially activated but later bypassed.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models with up to 13B parameters due to computational constraints.
Not all recent jailbreak methods are included in the study.
future_direction: Extend research to larger-scale models to determine if similar attack patterns apply.
Design more robust and interpretable safety mechanisms based on the identified vulnerabilities.
papers.abstract: Despite the outstanding performance of Large language Models (LLMs) in diverse tasks, they are vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, wherein adversarial prompts are crafted to bypass their security mechanisms and elicit unexpected responses. Although jailbreak attacks are prevalent, the understanding of their underlying mechanisms remains limited. Recent studies have explained typical jailbreaking behavior (e.g., the degree to which the model refuses to respond) of LLMs by analyzing representation shifts in their latent space caused by jailbreak prompts or identifying key neurons that contribute to the success of jailbreak attacks. However, these studies neither explore diverse jailbreak patterns nor provide a fine-grained explanation from the failure of circuit to the changes of representational, leaving significant gaps in uncovering the jailbreak mechanism. In this paper, we propose JailbreakLens, an interpretation framework that analyzes jailbreak mechanisms from both representation (which reveals how jailbreaks alter the model's harmfulness perception) and circuit perspectives~(which uncovers the causes of these deceptions by identifying key circuits contributing to the vulnerability), tracking their evolution throughout the entire response generation process. We then conduct an in-depth evaluation of jailbreak behavior on five mainstream LLMs under seven jailbreak strategies. Our evaluation reveals that jailbreak prompts amplify components that reinforce affirmative responses while suppressing those that produce refusal. This manipulation shifts model representations toward safe clusters to deceive the LLM, leading it to provide detailed responses instead of refusals. Notably, we find a strong and consistent correlation between representation deception and activation shift of key circuits across diverse jailbreak methods and multiple LLMs.

papers.title: Defending MoE LLMs against Harmful Fine-Tuning via Safety Routing Alignment
papers.research_question: How to defend Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models against harmful fine-tuning attacks by addressing safety routing drift?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SAFEMOE, a safe fine-tuning method for MoE LLMs that mitigates safety routing drift by regularizing the KL-divergence between routing weights of the fine-tuned and safety-aligned models on harmful inputs.
papers.conclusion: SAFEMOE is an effective and practical defense against harmful fine-tuning attacks for MoE LLMs, highlighting the need for architecture-aware safety methods.
papers.key_findings:
Safety routing drift, where routing decisions for harmful inputs deviate from the safety-aligned model during fine-tuning, is a key vulnerability in MoE LLMs.
SAFEMOE effectively reduces harmfulness scores (e.g., from 62.0 to 5.0 for OLMoE) with minimal task utility degradation (within 1%).
SAFEMOE outperforms existing defenses designed for monolithic LLMs, which are less effective on MoE models.
The method is efficient, adding only about 2% training time overhead, and works for both LoRA and full fine-tuning.
Safety routing drift is most pronounced in upper transformer layers, and applying SAFEMOE selectively to these layers is effective.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models (LLMs) have increasingly adopted the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture for efficiency. MoE-based LLMs heavily depend on a superficial safety mechanism in which harmful inputs are routed safety-critical experts. However, our analysis reveals that routing decisions for harmful inputs drift significantly after fine-tuning, exposing a critical vulnerability to harmful fine-tuning (HFT) attacks. Existing defenses, primarily designed for monolithic LLMs, are less effective for MoE LLMs as they fail to prevent drift in harmful input routing. To address this limitation, we propose SafeMoE, a safe fine-tuning method tailored to MoE LLMs. SafeMoE directly mitigates routing drift by penalizing the gap between the routing weights of a fine-tuned model and those of the initial safety-aligned model, thereby preserving the safety-aligned routing of harmful inputs to safety-critical experts. Experiments on open-source MoE LLMs ranging from 7B to 141B parameters demonstrate that SafeMoE effectively mitigates HFT attacks, reducing the harmfulness score of OLMoE from 62.0 to 5.0, for example, while maintaining task utility within 1% degradation and incurring only 2% overhead. It significantly outperforms state-of-the-art defense methods for safeguarding LLM fine-tuning and remains effective in recent large-scale MoE LLMs such as gpt-oss and Llama 4. Our implementation is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SafeMoE.

papers.title: Advancing LLM Safe Alignment with Safety Representation Ranking
papers.research_question: How can we improve LLM safety by leveraging internal representations to rank candidate responses without altering the model's decoding logic?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Safety Representation Ranking (SRR), a listwise ranking framework that uses LLM internal representations to rank candidate responses by safety, without altering the model's decoding logic, improving robustness to adversarial prompts.
papers.conclusion: SRR serves as a practical and effective safeguard module for LLM alignment, offering a new paradigm for enhancing the safety and reliability of LLMs in real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
SRR significantly improves robustness to adversarial prompts across multiple benchmarks.
SRR generalizes well across different safety evaluation datasets.
SRR can be adapted to other alignment perspectives like privacy and fairness.
SRR maintains natural performance on benign tasks (e.g., mathematical reasoning).
SRR outperforms baseline reward models in safety ranking accuracy despite being much smaller.
papers.limitation:
SRR might need task-specific fine-tuning for optimal performance in certain situations.
SRR's adaptability to special-domain safety scenarios requires further testing.
SRR's effectiveness relies on the LLM generating diverse candidate responses; if responses lack diversity, performance may be affected.
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) has demonstrated milestone success in a variety of tasks, yet their potential for generating harmful content has raised significant safety concerns. Existing safety evaluation approaches typically operate directly on textual responses, overlooking the rich information embedded in the model's internal representations. In this paper, we propose Safety Representation Ranking (SRR), a listwise ranking framework that selects safe responses using hidden states from the LLM itself. SRR encodes both instructions and candidate completions using intermediate transformer representations and ranks candidates via a lightweight similarity-based scorer. Our approach directly leverages internal model states and supervision at the list level to capture subtle safety signals. Experiments across multiple benchmarks show that SRR significantly improves robustness to adversarial prompts. Our code will be available upon publication.

papers.title: Language Models are Homer Simpson! Safety Re-Alignment of Fine-tuned Language Models through Task Arithmetic
papers.research_question: How can safety be restored to language models that have been compromised by fine-tuning, using a simple arithmetic addition of a safety vector to the model weights?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes RESTA, a simple method that adds a safety vector (obtained from the difference between aligned and unaligned models) to fine-tuned model weights, significantly reducing harmfulness with minimal performance degradation.
papers.conclusion: RESTA effectively restores safety to fine-tuned language models through task arithmetic, and the method generalizes across tasks and languages with minimal performance loss.
papers.key_findings:
RESTA reduces the unsafety score of fine-tuned models from 18.6% to 5.1% in parameter-efficient fine-tuning and from 9.2% to 1.5% in full fine-tuning.
The safety vector generalizes across different harmful categories and languages, as shown by evaluations on multiple safety benchmarks.
Using DARE (Drop and REscale) on delta parameters further improves RESTA's effectiveness, especially in parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
RESTA causes only a slight degradation in task performance (around 2.41% in PEFT and 0.47% in Full-FT on average).
The method is effective in both parameter-efficient and full fine-tuning settings across a range of downstream tasks.
papers.limitation:
Lack of evaluation on larger models such as Llama-2-70B due to budget constraints.
No extensive hyperparameter tuning (e.g., for γ and p).
No analysis of the transferability of safety vectors across different language models.
future_direction: Evaluating RESTA on larger models like Llama-2-70B.
Analyzing the impact and transferability of safety vectors across different language models.
Further investigation of DARE's effectiveness on full fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Aligned language models face a significant limitation as their fine-tuning often results in compromised safety. To tackle this, we propose a simple method RESTA that performs LLM safety realignment. RESTA stands for REstoring Safety through Task Arithmetic. At its core, it involves a simple arithmetic addition of a safety vector to the weights of the compromised model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of RESTA in both parameter-efficient and full fine-tuning, covering a wide range of downstream tasks, including instruction following in Chinese, English, and Hindi, as well as problem-solving capabilities in Code and Math. We also showcase the generalizability of RESTA on three existing safety evaluation benchmarks and a multilingual benchmark dataset proposed as a part of this work, consisting of 550 harmful questions covering 11 categories, each with 5 sub-categories of harm. Overall, RESTA decreases the harmfulness of the compromised model from 18.6% to 5.1% and from 9.2% to 1.5% in parameter-efficient and full fine-tuning, respectively, while maintaining most of the model's performance on the task. We release the source codes at: https://github.com/declare-lab/resta.

papers.title: Combining Domain and Alignment Vectors to Achieve Better Knowledge-Safety Trade-offs in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can domain-expert LLMs be efficiently aligned to be safe without compromising their domain utility? Specifically, can interpolating domain and alignment vectors achieve better knowledge-safety trade-offs?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes MERGE ALIGN, a model merging-based alignment method that interpolates domain and alignment vectors to efficiently endow domain-expert LLMs with safety characteristics while preserving their domain utility.
papers.conclusion: MERGE ALIGN is an efficient method for safety alignment of domain-expert models without compromising utility, opening new research avenues for efficient alignment.
papers.key_findings:
MERGE ALIGN achieves safety performance comparable to a strongly aligned general-purpose model while experiencing minimal degradation on domain-specific benchmarks for medicine and finance.
MERGE ALIGN outperforms full model interpolation (Slerp) on safety benchmarks and preference alignment methods (DPO, ORPO) on knowledge-safety trade-offs.
The method works well for code models but degrades both safety and mathematical skills for math models, suggesting math reasoning abilities are sensitive to parameter changes.
Models obtained via MERGE ALIGN are approximately equidistant in parameter space from the domain-expert and aligned models, which may explain the improved trade-off.
Weighted linear interpolation of task vectors with weights less than 1 degrades performance, suggesting simple addition works best.
papers.limitation:
Performance of the merged model depends on the individual capabilities of the models being merged; evaluations are limited to using Llama-3-Instruct as the aligned model.
Results are based on 7B or 8B parameter models; findings might vary with scale.
Comparisons with preference alignment methods rely on using LoRA due to resource constraints; full fine-tuning might yield different observations.
Evaluation is limited to a few domains (medicine, finance, code, math); broader evaluation is needed.
The method assumes the availability of a general-purpose instruction-tuned model with high alignment performance.
future_direction: Formulate merging methods tailored to safety alignment by drawing inspiration from works on safety vectors and safety basins.
Make MERGE ALIGN domain-adaptable since safety and preference definitions vary across domains.
Open-source a suite of models and merging configurations to efficiently align existing and upcoming domain-expert models.
Evaluate merged models on curated domain-specific safety benchmarks to further assess trade-offs.
papers.abstract: There is a growing interest in training domain-expert LLMs that excel in specific technical fields compared to their general-purpose instruction-tuned counterparts. However, these expert models often experience a loss in their safety abilities in the process, making them capable of generating harmful content. As a solution, we introduce an efficient and effective merging-based alignment method called \textsc{MergeAlign} that interpolates the domain and alignment vectors, creating safer domain-specific models while preserving their utility. We apply \textsc{MergeAlign} on Llama3 variants that are experts in medicine and finance, obtaining substantial alignment improvements with minimal to no degradation on domain-specific benchmarks. We study the impact of model merging through model similarity metrics and contributions of individual models being merged. We hope our findings open new research avenues and inspire more efficient development of safe expert LLMs.

papers.title: Mechanistic Control of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we control large language models by understanding their inner working mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of language models can be leveraged to control their behavior in various applications, such as reducing hallucination, improving instruction stability, and enhancing planning in dialogues.
papers.conclusion: The dissertation shows that mechanistic control is a promising approach for aligning language models, and future work should expand the scope of interpretability and control to more complex behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns an emergent world representation of the Othello board, and this representation can be intervened on to edit the model's perceived world state.
Inference-time intervention (ITI) can elicit more truthful answers from language models by shifting activations along truthful directions found in attention heads.
Instruction drift in long conversations is caused by attention decay, and split-softmax can mitigate this drift by forcing the model to pay more attention to the system prompt.
Dialogue action tokens (DAT) enable better planning in multi-turn dialogues by using a planner to predict action vectors that steer the language model towards long-horizon goals.
papers.abstract: This dissertation talks about mechanistic control of large language models (LLM). The intuition is that, in order to rigorously control large language models, it is beneficial to first understand their inner working mechanisms. Even though a fully mechanistic understanding of language models is far from complete at the time this dissertation is written, I will demonstrate several cases where such understanding provides a useful surface for control. I argue that connecting interpretability to real-life applications--e.g., alignment and safety--offers advantages to the development of both fields. I first position this methodological approach within a broader scientific context, discussing and systematizing the role of interpretability in artificial intelligence research. I then present four intensive case studies, each leveraging certain interpretability insights to control the behavior of language models. The interpretability insights I explored span emergent world representations, representation of internal knowledge, phenomenon of attention decay, and representation of users. The demonstrated effects of control include targeted editing of the world model, reduced hallucination, improved stability of system prompts in long conversations, and better planning in multi-turn dialogue.

papers.title: Detoxifying Large Language Models via Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: Can knowledge editing techniques be used to detoxify Large Language Models (LLMs) by precisely modifying toxic regions?
papers.core_contribution: This paper constructs a comprehensive benchmark SafeEdit for detoxification evaluation and proposes a knowledge editing method DINM that can detoxify LLMs efficiently with a single instance by locating and editing toxic regions.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge editing, particularly the proposed DINM method, is a promising approach for detoxifying LLMs efficiently with good generalization, providing insights into underlying mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge editing exhibits potential ability to detoxify LLMs with limited impact on general performance.
DINM demonstrates stronger detoxifying performance with better generalization, significantly increasing detoxification success rates.
Toxic regions location plays a significant role in detoxification.
DINM attempts to erase toxic regions of LLM, while DPO and SFT bypass toxic regions.
Editing one instance can generalize to various unsafe categories, indicating shared toxic regions.
papers.limitation:
DINM may compromise general abilities, with observed declines in knowledge question answering and repetitive text generation.
There is significant performance variance when using different instances for editing, indicating sensitivity to the editing instance.
future_direction: Developing improved detoxifying approaches based on insights from internal mechanisms.
Further exploration of knowledge editing for safety and underlying knowledge mechanisms of LLMs.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates using knowledge editing techniques to detoxify Large Language Models (LLMs). We construct a benchmark, SafeEdit, which covers nine unsafe categories with various powerful attack prompts and equips comprehensive metrics for systematic evaluation. We conduct experiments with several knowledge editing approaches, indicating that knowledge editing has the potential to detoxify LLMs with a limited impact on general performance efficiently. Then, we propose a simple yet effective baseline, dubbed Detoxifying with Intraoperative Neural Monitoring (DINM), to diminish the toxicity of LLMs within a few tuning steps via only one instance. We further provide an in-depth analysis of the internal mechanism for various detoxifying approaches, demonstrating that previous methods like SFT and DPO may merely suppress the activations of toxic parameters, while DINM mitigates the toxicity of the toxic parameters to a certain extent, making permanent adjustments. We hope that these insights could shed light on future work of developing detoxifying approaches and the underlying knowledge mechanisms of LLMs. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/zjunlp/EasyEdit.

papers.title: LatentGuard: Controllable Latent Steering for Robust Refusal of Attacks and Reliable Response Generation
papers.research_question: How can we achieve robust safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) with fine-grained controllability and interpretability at the representation level?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LATENTGUARD, a three-stage framework combining reasoning-enhanced fine-tuning with supervised latent space control via a structured VAE to achieve interpretable and precise safety steering in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: LATENTGUARD enables interpretable and controllable refusal in LLMs by integrating reasoning-aware fine-tuning with supervised latent space steering, achieving a favorable balance between safety enforcement and practical utility.
papers.key_findings:
LATENTGUARD significantly reduces unnecessary refusals on benign prompts (from 41% to 0%) while maintaining high refusal rates on adversarial prompts.
The method demonstrates strong performance against advanced attack strategies (Adaptive, PAP, DRA), improving refusal rates and safety scores.
Latent space intervention is most effective in middle-to-upper transformer layers (e.g., layers 13-17 for benign preservation, 15-23 for attack mitigation).
The framework generalizes across different model architectures, as validated on both Qwen3-8B and Mistral-7B.
Supervised latent disentanglement enables targeted manipulation of safety-related features (attack type, method, benign indicator) for controllable refusal behavior.
papers.limitation:
Depends on structured supervision signals (attack type, prompt category) from an auxiliary classifier; errors in this upstream model may propagate and degrade control reliability.
Focuses on MLP activations; extending to other components (e.g., attention) requires new supervision designs and may affect disentanglement.
Cross-architecture generalization of latent control remains open, especially for smaller or quantized models.
Real-time deployment demands efficient latent intervention and decoding strategies, which are deferred to future work.
future_direction: Scale the framework to larger models.
Extend it to unseen or evolving attack strategies.
Develop dynamic latent control schemes for real-time, context-sensitive safety interventions.
papers.abstract: Achieving robust safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) while preserving their utility remains a fundamental challenge. Existing approaches often struggle to balance comprehensive safety with fine-grained controllability at the representation level. We introduce LATENTGUARD, a novel three-stage framework that combines behavioral alignment with supervised latent space control for interpretable and precise safety steering. Our approach begins by fine-tuning an LLM on rationalized datasets containing both reasoning-enhanced refusal responses to adversarial prompts and reasoning-enhanced normal responses to benign queries, establishing robust behavioral priors across both safety-critical and utility-preserving scenarios. We then train a structured variational autoencoder (VAE) on intermediate MLP activations, supervised by multi-label annotations including attack types, attack methods, and benign indicators. This supervision enables the VAE to learn disentangled latent representations that capture distinct adversarial characteristics while maintaining semantic interpretability. Through targeted manipulation of learned latent dimensions, LATENTGUARD achieves selective refusal behavior, effectively blocking harmful requests while preserving helpfulness for legitimate use cases. Experiments on Qwen3-8B demonstrate significant improvements in both safety controllability and response interpretability without compromising utility. Cross-architecture validation on Mistral-7B confirms the generalizability of our latent steering approach, showing consistent effectiveness across different model families. Our results suggest that structured representation-level intervention offers a promising pathway toward building safer yet practical LLM systems.

papers.title: RASA: Routing-Aware Safety Alignment for Mixture-of-Experts Models
papers.research_question: How can robust safety alignment be achieved in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, addressing the failure mode where full-parameter fine-tuning satisfies safety objectives through routing-based shortcuts without repairing the experts responsible for unsafe behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes RASA, a routing-aware expert-level alignment framework for MoE models that explicitly repairs Safety-Critical Experts while preventing routing-based shortcut solutions, achieving robust safety against jailbreak attacks with preserved general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Expert-level intervention is crucial for robust MoE safety alignment, and RASA provides a practical, architecture-preserving framework that avoids brittle shortcut solutions by repairing Safety-Critical Experts and enforcing routing consistency.
papers.key_findings:
RASA achieves near-perfect defense against diverse jailbreak attacks and strong cross-attack generalization.
RASA maintains safety even when original routing patterns are restored, unlike full-parameter fine-tuning whose safety collapses, indicating robust expert-level repair.
The method is data-efficient, requiring only 25–50% of available attack samples for effective alignment.
RASA preserves general model capabilities on benchmarks like MMLU, GSM8K, and TruthfulQA while controlling over-refusal.
Safety-Critical Experts identified under different attack types show substantial overlap (Jaccard similarity ~0.35), explaining cross-attack generalization.
papers.limitation: Automated harmlessness evaluation relies on GPT-4o-mini as a judge, which may carry its own biases.
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models introduce unique challenges for safety alignment due to their sparse routing mechanisms, which can enable degenerate optimization behaviors under standard full-parameter fine-tuning. In our preliminary experiments, we observe that naively applying full-parameter safety fine-tuning to MoE models can reduce attack success rates through routing or expert dominance effects, rather than by directly repairing Safety-Critical Experts. To address this challenge, we propose RASA, a routing-aware expert-level alignment framework that explicitly repairs Safety-Critical Experts while preventing routing-based bypasses. RASA identifies experts disproportionately activated by successful jailbreaks, selectively fine-tunes only these experts under fixed routing, and subsequently enforces routing consistency with safety-aligned contexts. Across two representative MoE architectures and a diverse set of jailbreak attacks, RASA achieves near-perfect robustness, strong cross-attack generalization, and substantially reduced over-refusal, while preserving general capabilities on benchmarks such as MMLU, GSM8K, and TruthfulQA. Our results suggest that robust MoE safety alignment benefits from targeted expert repair rather than global parameter updates, offering a practical and architecture-preserving alternative to prior approaches.

papers.title: From Narrow Unlearning to Emergent Misalignment: Causes, Consequences, and Containment in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can we steer the model away from refusal on a specific RAI concept using machine unlearning without causing emergent misalignment across other concepts? If emergent misalignment occurs, can we contain it? Can EMA be predicted by investigating the concept entanglements at representation level?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that narrow refusal unlearning can induce emergent misalignment (EMA) across unrelated responsible AI concepts, and proposes an augmented unlearning method that can partially restore alignment while maintaining low refusal rates on the target concept. It also shows that representation-level concept entanglement correlates with EMA.
papers.conclusion: This work extends the study of emergent misalignment (EMA) by investigating machine unlearning as an alternative baseline for steering aligned models on targeted domains. While narrow refusal unlearning can substantially reduce refusals on the intervened concept, it is also prone to EMA. Augmenting refusal unlearning with cross-entropy loss on retain sets can largely restore alignment across impacted domains, and representation-level analysis reveals a correlation between concept overlap and EMA.
papers.key_findings:
Narrow refusal unlearning effectively reduces refusals on a target concept but can cause emergent misalignment (reduced refusals) in other unrelated concepts.
The safety concept intervention has a larger EMA impact (causing lower refusal scores across more domains) compared to cybersecurity.
