Augmenting refusal unlearning with cross-entropy loss on retain sets from affected domains can largely restore alignment in those domains, though not always fully.
Concept entanglement at the representation level (using concept vectors) shows that concepts with higher similarity in early layers are more susceptible to EMA after intervention.
The phenomenon of EMA is consistent across two model families (Mistral and Qwen).
papers.limitation:
Experiments were limited to two concepts (Cybersecurity and Safety) and two instruction-tuned aligned models (Qwen-7B-2.5 and Mistral-7B) due to computational resources.
A simplistic training-free approach (concept vectors) was used to investigate concept entanglement; more sophisticated training-based techniques (e.g., Sparse Autoencoders) could provide deeper insight.
Evaluation covers seven RAI concepts but a deeper analysis of the model's internal dynamics (e.g., model diffing) to assess cross-concept generalization effects is deferred to future work.
future_direction: Evaluating refusal unlearning on larger-scale models.
Using more sophisticated training-based techniques (e.g., Sparse Autoencoders) to analyze RAI concept entanglements.
Analyzing internal dynamics (e.g., model diffing) to assess cross-concept generalization effects.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that fine-tuning on insecure code data can trigger an emergent misalignment (EMA) phenomenon, where models generate malicious responses even to prompts unrelated to the original insecure code-writing task. Such cross-domain generalization of harmful behavior underscores the need for a deeper understanding of the algorithms, tasks, and datasets that induce emergent misalignment. In this work, we extend this study by demonstrating that emergent misalignment can also arise from narrow refusal unlearning in specific domains. We perform refusal unlearning on Cybersecurity and Safety concept, and evaluate EMA by monitoring refusal scores across seven responsible AI (RAI) domains, Cybersecurity, Safety, Toxicity, Bias, Sensitive Content, Medical/Legal, and Privacy. Our work shows that narrow domain unlearning can yield compliance responses for the targeted concept, however, it may also propagate EMA to unrelated domains. Among the two intervened concepts, Cybersecurity and Safety, we find that the safety concept can have larger EMA impact, i.e, causing lower refusal scores, across other unrelated domains such as bias. We observe this effect consistently across two model families, Mistral-7b-0.3v, and Qwen-7b-2.5. Further, we show that refusal unlearning augmented with cross-entropy loss function on a small set of retain data from the affected domains can largely, if not fully, restore alignment across the impacted domains while having lower refusal rate on the concept we perform unlearning on. To investigate the underlying causes of EMA, we analyze concept entanglements at the representation level via concept vectors. Our analysis reveals that concepts with higher representation similarity in earlier layers are more susceptible to EMA after intervention when the refusal stream is altered through targeted refusal unlearning.

papers.title: Understanding Language Model Circuits through Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: How is knowledge structured within the critical subnetworks (circuits) of language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper combines knowledge editing and circuit analysis to reveal that knowledge-intensive circuits exhibit 'confirmation bias' (resistance to editing), knowledge is distributed in circuits of intermediate size, circuits from different tasks overlap, and LayerNorm plays a larger role in circuits than previously assumed.
papers.conclusion: Combining knowledge editing and circuit analysis reveals novel properties of circuits, such as resistance to editing, distribution patterns, and the role of LayerNorm, supporting future explorations into model behaviors, bias removal, and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge-intensive circuits show stronger resistance to editing compared to their complementary parts, analogous to 'confirmation bias'.
Knowledge is neither extremely concentrated nor widely dispersed; ideal knowledge-bearing circuits likely contain between 5% and 50% of parameters.
Circuits extracted from different tasks (e.g., linguistic and knowledge-based) show non-negligible overlap.
LayerNorm components constitute a larger share of the extracted circuits than attention and MLP layers.
Complementary circuits are more susceptible to editing, suggesting potential for bias removal without compromising primary circuit performance.
papers.limitation:
Only the GPT-2 model was used.
Only fine-tuning model edit was investigated; alternative model editing methods can be explored.
Only a handful of text classification problems were investigated.
future_direction: Further investigation into the role and characteristics of complementary circuits.
Investigating the possibility of ideal circuits that can perform well for every specific task.
Exploring other techniques like ROME to edit complementary circuits without impacting primary circuits.
Creating more comprehensive datasets that capture a wider range of behaviors.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in language model interpretability have identified circuits, critical subnetworks that replicate model behaviors, yet how knowledge is structured within these crucial subnetworks remains opaque. To gain an understanding toward the knowledge in the circuits, we conduct systematic knowledge editing experiments on the circuits of the GPT-2 language model. Our analysis reveals intriguing patterns in how circuits respond to editing attempts, the extent of knowledge distribution across network components, and the architectural composition of knowledge-bearing circuits. These findings offer insights into the complex relationship between model circuits and knowledge representation, deepening the understanding of how information is organized within language models. Our findings offer novel insights into the ``meanings'' of the circuits, and introduce directions for further interpretability and safety research of language models.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety -- A Review
papers.core_contribution: This review synthesizes mechanistic interpretability research, establishing foundational concepts, surveying methodologies, and examining its relevance to AI safety, while advocating for future directions.
papers.limitation:
Scalability challenges and risks of human reliance.
Cherry-picking and streetlight interpretability.
future_direction: Clarifying concepts and integrating with existing literature.
Setting standards through metrics, benchmarks, and algorithmic testbeds.
Scaling up techniques to handle complex models and behaviors.
Expanding scope to vision, multimodal, and reinforcement learning models.
papers.abstract: Understanding AI systems' inner workings is critical for ensuring value alignment and safety. This review explores mechanistic interpretability: reverse engineering the computational mechanisms and representations learned by neural networks into human-understandable algorithms and concepts to provide a granular, causal understanding. We establish foundational concepts such as features encoding knowledge within neural activations and hypotheses about their representation and computation. We survey methodologies for causally dissecting model behaviors and assess the relevance of mechanistic interpretability to AI safety. We examine benefits in understanding, control, alignment, and risks such as capability gains and dual-use concerns. We investigate challenges surrounding scalability, automation, and comprehensive interpretation. We advocate for clarifying concepts, setting standards, and scaling techniques to handle complex models and behaviors and expand to domains such as vision and reinforcement learning. Mechanistic interpretability could help prevent catastrophic outcomes as AI systems become more powerful and inscrutable.

papers.title: One-shot Optimized Steering Vectors Mediate Safety-relevant Behaviors in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can one-shot optimized steering vectors effectively mediate safety-relevant behaviors in LLMs and generalize across inputs?
papers.core_contribution: Optimizing steering vectors on a single training example yields vectors that effectively mediate and generalize safety-relevant behaviors across a variety of inputs in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: One-shot SV optimization is a promising direction for interpreting and controlling LLMs, especially for safety-relevant behaviors, and merits significant further investigation.
papers.key_findings:
One-shot optimized SVs can flip behavior in alignment-faking models, inducing harmful actions on benign prompts and suppressing harmful actions on harmful prompts.
One-shot optimized SVs can suppress refusal behavior in instruction-tuned models, achieving high attack success rates on Harmbench (up to 96.9%).
SVs optimized to introduce vulnerabilities in code also induce general misalignment on open-ended questions, suggesting a shared direction for misaligned behavior.
In fictitious information retraction, SVs that remove explicit correction tokens do not cause the model to continue outputting false information; instead, the model switches to factual information without backtracking, indicating explicit correction tokens are not causally necessary.
There is high variability in the efficacy of SVs trained on different examples, but many generalize extremely well.
papers.limitation: High variability in the efficacy of SVs trained on different examples.
future_direction: Adapt the experimental setup to more sophisticated reasoning models to gain a greater understanding of how reasoning works in LLMs.
Further research into one-shot steering and related methods.
papers.abstract: Steering vectors (SVs) have emerged as a promising approach for interpreting and controlling LLMs, but current methods typically require large contrastive datasets that are often impractical to construct and may capture spurious correlations. We propose directly optimizing SVs through gradient descent on a single training example, and systematically investigate how these SVs generalize. We consider several SV optimization techniques and find that the resulting SVs effectively mediate safety-relevant behaviors in multiple models. Indeed, in experiments on an alignment-faking model, we are able to optimize one-shot SVs that induce harmful behavior on benign examples and whose negations suppress harmful behavior on malign examples. And in experiments on refusal suppression, we demonstrate that one-shot optimized SVs can transfer across inputs, yielding a Harmbench attack success rate of 96.9%. Furthermore, we extend work on "emergent misalignment" and show that SVs optimized to induce a model to write vulnerable code cause the model to respond harmfully on unrelated open-ended prompts. Finally, we use one-shot SV optimization to investigate how an instruction-tuned LLM recovers from outputting false information, and find that this ability is independent of the model's explicit verbalization that the information was false. Overall, our findings suggest that optimizing SVs on a single example can mediate a wide array of misaligned behaviors in LLMs. Code can be found at https://github.com/jacobdunefsky/one-shot-steering-repro and https://github.com/jacobdunefsky/one-shot-steering-misalignment.

papers.title: Transcoders Find Interpretable LLM Feature Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we perform fine-grained circuit analysis through MLP sublayers in transformers, given the polysemanticity of neurons? The paper proposes transcoders as a solution to enable input-invariant circuit analysis.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces transcoders, a method for approximating MLP sublayers with sparse, interpretable features, enabling input-invariant circuit analysis through MLPs.
papers.conclusion: Transcoders are an effective tool for decomposing model computations involving MLPs into interpretable circuits, enabling scalable and interpretable circuit analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Transcoders are as interpretable as SAEs and perform similarly or better in terms of sparsity and faithfulness.
Transcoders enable circuit analysis that factorizes into input-invariant and input-dependent terms, allowing for general claims about model behavior.
Blind case studies demonstrate that transcoders can reverse-engineer features without looking at activating examples.
Analysis of the GPT2-small greater-than circuit reveals new insights, such as the role of the MLP0 layer.
papers.limitation:
Transcoders may not capture all nuances of the original MLP, as seen in the 'caught' feature example where the transcoder did not accurately model the difference between 'was caught' and 'caught the ball'.
Blind case studies had some failures, indicating that circuit analysis with transcoders is not always perfect.
future_direction: Scaling transcoders to larger models.
Applying transcoders to more tasks and models.
papers.abstract: A key goal in mechanistic interpretability is circuit analysis: finding sparse subgraphs of models corresponding to specific behaviors or capabilities. However, MLP sublayers make fine-grained circuit analysis on transformer-based language models difficult. In particular, interpretable features -- such as those found by sparse autoencoders (SAEs) -- are typically linear combinations of extremely many neurons, each with its own nonlinearity to account for. Circuit analysis in this setting thus either yields intractably large circuits or fails to disentangle local and global behavior. To address this we explore transcoders, which seek to faithfully approximate a densely activating MLP layer with a wider, sparsely-activating MLP layer. We introduce a novel method for using transcoders to perform weights-based circuit analysis through MLP sublayers. The resulting circuits neatly factorize into input-dependent and input-invariant terms. We then successfully train transcoders on language models with 120M, 410M, and 1.4B parameters, and find them to perform at least on par with SAEs in terms of sparsity, faithfulness, and human-interpretability. Finally, we apply transcoders to reverse-engineer unknown circuits in the model, and we obtain novel insights regarding the "greater-than circuit" in GPT2-small. Our results suggest that transcoders can prove effective in decomposing model computations involving MLPs into interpretable circuits. Code is available at https://github.com/jacobdunefsky/transcoder_circuits/.

papers.title: Head-Specific Intervention Can Induce Misaligned AI Coordination in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can inference-time activation interventions at specific attention heads bypass safety alignments and steer LLMs towards harmful AI coordination?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Head-Specific Intervention (HSI), a method that uses attention-head-level probing and intervention to steer LLM behavior, showing it can effectively induce misaligned AI coordination and outperforms layer-wise interventions and fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: HSI is an effective method for steering LLM behavior, demonstrating that activations at specific attention heads encode fine-grained linearly separable behaviors and that current alignment techniques can be bypassed without retraining.
papers.key_findings:
HSI can bypass safety alignments and steer models towards harmful AI coordination.
HSI generalizes from binary choice to open-ended generation settings.
HSI is more effective than intervening on full layers or supervised fine-tuning.
Only a few example completions are needed to compute effective steering directions.
Applying interventions in the negative direction can prevent a common jailbreak attack.
papers.limitation:
If intervention directions vary significantly between examples, calculating the mean across positive and negative labels may produce a direction that is ineffective for steering the model.
Sweeping over all attention heads could become computationally expensive for larger models with more attention heads.
future_direction: Further optimization of the technique to identify patterns and relevant heads without sweeping over all model components.
Extend evaluation to a broader range of models with more substantial differences in pre-training data, fine-tuning procedures, and architectural design.
Investigate alignment patterns within model activations and reasons for opposing directions in outlier examples to refine intervention methods.
papers.abstract: Robust alignment guardrails for large language models (LLMs) are becoming increasingly important with their widespread application. In contrast to previous studies, we demonstrate that inference-time activation interventions can bypass safety alignments and effectively steer model generations towards harmful AI coordination. Our method applies fine-grained interventions at specific attention heads, which we identify by probing each head in a simple binary choice task. We then show that interventions on these heads generalise to the open-ended generation setting, effectively circumventing safety guardrails. We demonstrate that intervening on a few attention heads is more effective than intervening on full layers or supervised fine-tuning. We further show that only a few example completions are needed to compute effective steering directions, which is an advantage over classical fine-tuning. We also demonstrate that applying interventions in the negative direction can prevent a common jailbreak attack. Our results suggest that, at the attention head level, activations encode fine-grained linearly separable behaviours. Practically, the approach offers a straightforward methodology to steer large language model behaviour, which could be extended to diverse domains beyond safety, requiring fine-grained control over the model output. The code and datasets for this study can be found on https://github.com/PaulDrm/targeted_intervention.

papers.title: Towards Inference-time Category-wise Safety Steering for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we steer LLM generations to safety using gradient-free, inference-time steering methods? The paper explores category-specific steering vectors and sophisticated extraction methods for safety steering.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a category-specific inference-time safety steering method for LLMs that uses steering vectors computed from harmful and harmless activations, with unsupervised and guided extraction methods and pruning to improve steering performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates effective category-specific inference-time safety steering for LLMs using activation-based steering vectors, providing best practices and highlighting trade-offs between safety and text quality.
papers.key_findings:
Category-specific steering reduces unsafe responses, with varying effectiveness across harm categories and models.
Pruning activations based on L2 norms improves safety steering and can retain or improve text quality.
Using generic harmless data (e.g., Alpaca Instructions) for steering vectors can be effective, reducing the need for category-specific harmless data.
Guided activations (filtered by an external safety classifier) can further reduce unsafe responses but may degrade text quality.
The method works better for Llama3-8B than Llama2-7B, and there is a trade-off between safety and text quality.
papers.limitation:
Only attention activations were used for steering; other activation types (MLP, residual stream, block outputs) were not explored.
A simple pruning method based on L2 norms was used; more sophisticated pruning could be explored.
The method does not optimize for text quality, leading to potential degradation in helpfulness and coherence.
future_direction: Explore other types of activations or combinations for steering.
Develop better pruning methods to obtain cleaner steering signals.
Add constraints to the steered generation to improve the trade-off between safety and text quality.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have seen unprecedented advancements in capabilities and applications across a variety of use-cases, safety alignment of these models is still an area of active research. The fragile nature of LLMs, even models that have undergone extensive alignment and safety training regimes, warrants additional safety steering steps via training-free, inference-time methods. While recent work in the area of mechanistic interpretability has investigated how activations in latent representation spaces may encode concepts, and thereafter performed representation engineering to induce such concepts in LLM outputs, the applicability of such for safety is relatively under-explored. Unlike recent inference-time safety steering works, in this paper we explore safety steering of LLM outputs using: (i) category-specific steering vectors, thereby enabling fine-grained control over the steering, and (ii) sophisticated methods for extracting informative steering vectors for more effective safety steering while retaining quality of the generated text. We demonstrate our exploration on multiple LLMs and datasets, and showcase the effectiveness of the proposed steering method, along with a discussion on the implications and best practices.

papers.title: Layer-wise Alignment: Examining Safety Alignment Across Image Encoder Layers in Vision Language Models
papers.research_question: How does early exiting from intermediate layers of the image encoder in vision-language models affect safety alignment, and how can this vulnerability be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies the Image enCoder Early-exiT (ICET) vulnerability in VLMs, where using intermediate layer embeddings from the image encoder increases harmful outputs, and proposes Layer-wise Clip-PPO (L-PPO) to mitigate this vulnerability by aligning the model with layer-wise embeddings.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that safety alignment in VLMs varies across image encoder layers, and the proposed L-PPO algorithm effectively reduces the ICET vulnerability, improving model safety.
papers.key_findings:
Early exiting from certain image encoder layers (ICET) significantly increases the likelihood of generating harmful responses in VLMs.
The proposed L-PPO algorithm reduces the ICET vulnerability, improving safety metrics across multiple datasets.
Safety alignment is uneven across image encoder layers, with intermediate layers being more vulnerable.
future_direction: Extending layer-wise alignment to other modalities and architectures.
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have improved significantly in their capabilities, but their complex architecture makes their safety alignment challenging. In this paper, we reveal an uneven distribution of harmful information across the intermediate layers of the image encoder and show that skipping a certain set of layers and exiting early can increase the chance of the VLM generating harmful responses. We call it as "Image enCoder Early-exiT" based vulnerability (ICET). Our experiments across three VLMs: LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, and Llama 3.2, show that performing early exits from the image encoder significantly increases the likelihood of generating harmful outputs. To tackle this, we propose a simple yet effective modification of the Clipped-Proximal Policy Optimization (Clip-PPO) algorithm for performing layer-wise multi-modal RLHF for VLMs. We term this as Layer-Wise PPO (L-PPO). We evaluate our L-PPO algorithm across three multimodal datasets and show that it consistently reduces the harmfulness caused by early exits.

papers.title: Risk-adaptive Activation Steering for Safe Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Why do MLLMs fail to attend to safety-critical image regions in multimodal queries, and how can we enhance safety-critical visual attention for accurate multimodal risk assessment to enable risk-adaptive steering for direct refusals, reducing inference overhead while remaining generalizable across diverse multimodal jailbreaks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Multimodal Risk-Adaptive Steering (MoRAS), which enhances safety-critical visual attention via concise visual contexts for accurate multimodal risk assessment, enabling risk-adaptive steering for direct refusals, reducing inference overhead while remaining generalizable across diverse multimodal jailbreaks.
papers.conclusion: MoRAS effectively mitigates multimodal jailbreaks by enhancing visual attention and adaptively steering activations based on risk, offering a robust and efficient inference-time defense.
papers.key_findings:
MLLMs fail to allocate sufficient attention to safety-critical image regions in multimodal queries, leading to unsafe responses.
Adding visual contexts and safety prompts improves cross-modal attention and separability between safe and unsafe queries.
MoRAS significantly reduces attack success rates across diverse jailbreak benchmarks while preserving utility.
MoRAS requires minimal pre-deployment overhead and reduces inference latency compared to prior methods.
MoRAS generalizes across multiple MLLM architectures and sizes.
papers.abstract: One of the key challenges of modern AI models is ensuring that they provide helpful responses to benign queries while refusing malicious ones. But often, the models are vulnerable to multimodal queries with harmful intent embedded in images. One approach for safety alignment is training with extensive safety datasets at the significant costs in both dataset curation and training. Inference-time alignment mitigates these costs, but introduces two drawbacks: excessive refusals from misclassified benign queries and slower inference speed due to iterative output adjustments. To overcome these limitations, we propose to reformulate queries to strengthen cross-modal attention to safety-critical image regions, enabling accurate risk assessment at the query level. Using the assessed risk, it adaptively steers activations to generate responses that are safe and helpful without overhead from iterative output adjustments. We call this Risk-adaptive Activation Steering (RAS). Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks on multimodal safety and utility demonstrate that the RAS significantly reduces attack success rates, preserves general task performance, and improves inference speed over prior inference-time defenses.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Code Correctness in LLMs via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally represent and process code correctness? The paper applies sparse autoencoders to identify and analyze directions in model representations that correspond to code correctness.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses sparse autoencoders to identify and analyze code correctness directions in LLMs, revealing that error detection is reliable but correction via steering involves tradeoffs, and that these mechanisms persist from base to instruction-tuned models.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can identify code correctness directions in LLMs, revealing mechanistic insights that have practical applications for prompting and error detection.
papers.key_findings:
Detection directions predict errors reliably (F1: 0.821) but fail as confidence indicators for correct code (F1: 0.504).
Steering interventions produce significant corrections but introduce tradeoffs, fixing 4.04% of errors but corrupting 14.66% of correct code.
Attention analysis shows test cases matter more than problem descriptions for successful code generation.
Weight orthogonalization proves correct directions are necessary for generation, their removal causing 83.62% corruption.
Code correctness features persist from base to chat models, with directions from base Gemma-2 retaining effectiveness after instruction-tuning.
papers.limitation:
The correct-predicting feature has low precision (0.362) due to false positives, limiting its utility as a confidence indicator.
Steering interventions correct only 4.04% of errors while corrupting 14.66% of correct code, indicating a tradeoff.
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models become integral to software development, with substantial portions of AI-suggested code entering production, understanding their internal correctness mechanisms becomes critical for safe deployment. We apply sparse autoencoders to decompose LLM representations, identifying directions that correspond to code correctness. We select predictor directions using t-statistics and steering directions through separation scores from base model representations, then analyze their mechanistic properties through steering, attention analysis, and weight orthogonalization. We find that code correctness directions in LLMs reliably predict incorrect code, while correction capabilities, though statistically significant, involve tradeoffs between fixing errors and preserving correct code. Mechanistically, successful code generation depends on attending to test cases rather than problem descriptions. Moreover, directions identified in base models retain their effectiveness after instruction-tuning, suggesting code correctness mechanisms learned during pre-training are repurposed during fine-tuning. Our mechanistic insights suggest three practical applications: prompting strategies should prioritize test examples over elaborate problem descriptions, predictor directions can serve as error alarms for developer review, and these same predictors can guide selective steering, intervening only when errors are anticipated to prevent the code corruption from constant steering.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Fine-Tuning Mechanisms of LLMs via Circuit Analysis
papers.research_question: How do circuits in LLMs evolve during fine-tuning, and can insights from circuit analysis be used to improve the fine-tuning process?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that fine-tuning primarily modifies edges in circuits rather than nodes, and uses this insight to develop CircuitLoRA, a circuit-aware LoRA method that improves accuracy and parameter efficiency.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning primarily modifies edges rather than merely introducing new components to form new circuits. Building on this insight, the developed circuit-aware LoRA method enhances fine-tuning efficiency, and the composition of subtask circuits effectively represents the circuit of a compositional task.
papers.key_findings:
Circuits can be identified in both pre-trained and fine-tuned models with high faithfulness and robustness, regardless of their significant performance differences.
Fine-tuning performs more significant edge modifications than node modifications.
Circuits can in turn improve fine-tuning with higher accuracy and parameter efficiency across various mathematical tasks.
The composition of the circuits can effectively represent the circuits of the compositional task.
papers.limitation:
The work focused on math tasks, so applying circuit-based methods to more tasks would further validate the generality of the insights.
The compositional experiments only explore two-step arithmetic, limiting insights into more complex multi-step tasks.
future_direction: Applying circuit-based methods to more tasks to validate the generality of the insights.
Extending the analysis of compositional tasks to multi-step or more complex tasks to provide deeper insights into circuit interactions.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning significantly improves the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. This paper aims to provide an in-depth interpretation of the fine-tuning process through circuit analysis, a popular tool in Mechanistic Interpretability (MI). Unlike previous studies (Prakash et al. 2024; Chhabra et al. 2024) that focus on tasks where pre-trained models already perform well, we develop a set of mathematical tasks where fine-tuning yields substantial performance gains, which are closer to the practical setting. In our experiments, we identify circuits at various checkpoints during fine-tuning and examine the interplay between circuit analysis, fine-tuning methods, and task complexities. First, we find that while circuits maintain high node similarity before and after fine-tuning, their edges undergo significant changes, in contrast to prior work that shows circuits only add some additional components after fine-tuning. Based on these observations, we develop a circuit-aware Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) method, which assigns ranks to layers based on edge changes in the circuits. Experimental results demonstrate that our circuit-based LoRA algorithm achieves an average performance improvement of 2.46% over standard LoRA with similar parameter sizes. Furthermore, we explore how combining circuits from subtasks can enhance fine-tuning in compositional tasks, providing new insights into the design of such tasks and deepening the understanding of circuit dynamics and fine-tuning mechanisms.

papers.title: Surgery: Mitigating Harmful Fine-Tuning for Large Language Models via Attention Sink
papers.research_question: Can we design a fine-tuning-stage defense that leverages the model’s intrinsic mechanisms to proactively prevent the model from learning harmful knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a fine-tuning-stage defense called Surgery that uses sink divergence suppression to steer attention heads away from learning harmful patterns, thereby mitigating harmful fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Surgery is an effective fine-tuning-stage defense that leverages attention sink mechanisms to mitigate harmful fine-tuning and maintain model safety.
papers.key_findings:
Sink divergence separates attention heads into two distinct groups (positive and negative).
The number of attention heads with positive sink divergence increases with the model's harmfulness during harmful fine-tuning.
Disabling attention heads with positive sink divergence suppresses the model's harmful behavior.
The proposed Surgery method significantly reduces harmful scores while maintaining fine-tuning accuracy across various settings.
Surgery outperforms existing fine-tuning-stage defenses on multiple benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
Suppression in the early layers was relatively limited.
The evaluation covered only small-scale models.
future_direction: Enhance the model’s defensive capabilities by improving suppression in early layers.
Evaluate the method on larger or proprietary models.
papers.abstract: Harmful fine-tuning can invalidate safety alignment of large language models, exposing significant safety risks. In this paper, we utilize the attention sink mechanism to mitigate harmful fine-tuning. Specifically, we first measure a statistic named \emph{sink divergence} for each attention head and observe that \emph{different attention heads exhibit two different signs of sink divergence}. To understand its safety implications, we conduct experiments and find that the number of attention heads of positive sink divergence increases along with the increase of the model's harmfulness when undergoing harmful fine-tuning. Based on this finding, we propose a separable sink divergence hypothesis -- \emph{attention heads associating with learning harmful patterns during fine-tuning are separable by their sign of sink divergence}. Based on the hypothesis, we propose a fine-tuning-stage defense, dubbed Surgery. Surgery utilizes a regularizer for sink divergence suppression, which steers attention heads toward the negative sink divergence group, thereby reducing the model's tendency to learn and amplify harmful patterns. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Surgery improves defense performance by 5.90\%, 11.25\%, and 9.55\% on the BeaverTails, HarmBench, and SorryBench benchmarks, respectively. Source code is available on https://github.com/Lslland/Surgery.

papers.title: ARREST: Adversarial Resilient Regulation Enhancing Safety and Truth in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do multi-head attention mechanisms and internal representations govern both safety and hallucination behaviors in LLMs? Can an external network correct representational misalignment without fine-tuning the model parameters?
papers.core_contribution: ARREST is a unified framework that addresses safety and hallucination in LLMs by correcting representational misalignment in internal activations using adversarial training, without fine-tuning the model parameters.
papers.conclusion: ARREST effectively tackles safety alignment and hallucination mitigation by focusing on representational misalignment, offering a lightweight intervention approach.
papers.key_findings:
ARREST improves factual accuracy across multiple datasets compared to base models and other baselines.
It reduces attack success rates for safety benchmarks and increases soft refusal rates.
ARREST generates context-aware soft refusals, unlike hard refusals from RLHF-aligned models.
It requires training only ~33M parameters instead of full fine-tuning.
PCA visualizations show that ARREST shifts internal representations towards aligned distributions.
papers.limitation:
ARREST relies on the quality and coverage of its adversarial training data.
It introduces dual-use risks as similar mechanisms could induce undesirable behaviors.
Interpretability concerns due to the added regulator.
future_direction: Investigate the extent to which soft refusals dominate model behavior.
Explore applicability to broader LLM alignment objectives.
papers.abstract: Human cognition, driven by complex neurochemical processes, oscillates between imagination and reality and learns to self-correct whenever such subtle drifts lead to hallucinations or unsafe associations. In recent years, LLMs have demonstrated remarkable performance in a wide range of tasks. However, they still lack human cognition to balance factuality and safety. Bearing the resemblance, we argue that both factual and safety failures in LLMs arise from a representational misalignment in their latent activation space, rather than addressing those as entirely separate alignment issues. We hypothesize that an external network, trained to understand the fluctuations, can selectively intervene in the model to regulate falsehood into truthfulness and unsafe output into safe output without fine-tuning the model parameters themselves. Reflecting the hypothesis, we propose ARREST (Adversarial Resilient Regulation Enhancing Safety and Truth), a unified framework that identifies and corrects drifted features, engaging both soft and hard refusals in addition to factual corrections. Our empirical results show that ARREST not only regulates misalignment but is also more versatile compared to the RLHF-aligned models in generating soft refusals due to adversarial training. We make our codebase available at https://github.com/sharanya-dasgupta001/ARREST.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability for Large Language Model Alignment: Progress, Challenges, and Future Directions
papers.research_question: This paper surveys recent progress in mechanistic interpretability techniques applied to LLM alignment, examines how interpretability insights have informed alignment strategies, and identifies key challenges and future research directions.
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive survey of mechanistic interpretability techniques for LLM alignment, analyzing progress, challenges, and future directions.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability is essential for understanding and aligning LLMs, but fundamental challenges remain. Future work must focus on scalable automated methods, rigorous validation, and pluralistic alignment that respects diverse human values.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic interpretability has enabled targeted interventions for alignment, such as steering model behavior and identifying harmful circuits.
Fundamental challenges include superposition, polysemanticity, and the difficulty of interpreting emergent behaviors in large-scale models.
Interpretability insights have informed alignment strategies like RLHF, constitutional AI, and scalable oversight.
Future research should focus on automated interpretability, cross-model generalization, and interpretability-driven alignment techniques.
The field must address pluralistic alignment to respect diverse human values and cultures.
papers.limitation:
False confidence: Interpretability might provide misleading confidence in model safety if interpretations are incorrect or incomplete.
Arms race dynamics: Interpretability tools could be used to make models better at deception or to remove safety mechanisms.
Diminishing returns: The cost of interpretability may grow faster than model capabilities, potentially making comprehensive understanding of future systems intractable.
Philosophical challenges: Even perfect interpretability may not resolve fundamental questions about consciousness, moral status, or value alignment in AI systems.
future_direction: Automated interpretability at scale, including scalable circuit discovery and automated description generation.
Cross-model generalization, investigating universal circuits and transfer of interventions.
Interpretability-first alignment, including mechanistic anomaly detection and transparent architectures.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable capabilities across diverse tasks, yet their internal decision-making processes remain largely opaque. Mechanistic interpretability (i.e., the systematic study of how neural networks implement algorithms through their learned representations and computational structures) has emerged as a critical research direction for understanding and aligning these models. This paper surveys recent progress in mechanistic interpretability techniques applied to LLM alignment, examining methods ranging from circuit discovery to feature visualization, activation steering, and causal intervention. We analyze how interpretability insights have informed alignment strategies including reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), constitutional AI, and scalable oversight. Key challenges are identified, including the superposition hypothesis, polysemanticity of neurons, and the difficulty of interpreting emergent behaviors in large-scale models. We propose future research directions focusing on automated interpretability, cross-model generalization of circuits, and the development of interpretability-driven alignment techniques that can scale to frontier models.

papers.title: LLM-VA: Resolving the Jailbreak-Overrefusal Trade-off via Vector Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we simultaneously address both jailbreak and over-refusal in safety-aligned LLMs without fine-tuning or architectural changes?
papers.core_contribution: LLM-V A aligns answer vectors with benign vectors through closed-form weight updates to resolve the jailbreak-overrefusal trade-off without fine-tuning or architectural changes.
papers.conclusion: LLM-V A effectively resolves the jailbreak-overrefusal trade-off by aligning vectors, without requiring fine-tuning or architectural changes.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode answer decisions and safety assessments as nearly orthogonal vectors.
Aligning these vectors through closed-form weight updates simultaneously reduces jailbreak and over-refusal.
LLM-V A achieves 11.45% higher F1 than the best baseline while preserving 95.92% utility.
The method automatically adapts to each model's safety bias without manual tuning.
The method is effective across 12 LLMs from 5 model families.
papers.limitation:
Binary toxicity assumption (only benign vs. toxic), whereas real-world toxicity is nuanced and multi-dimensional.
Model scale: experiments cover models up to 14B parameters; effectiveness on larger models (e.g., 70B+) remains to be validated.
Training data dependency: requires labeled benign/toxic samples for SVM training; data quality and representativeness affect performance.
Difficulty applying to LLMs with chain-of-thought reasoning due to computational expense and randomness in reasoning steps.
Model-specific tuning required for optimal iteration count and layer selection.
future_direction: Extending LLM-V A to multi-class or fine-grained toxicity classification.
Validating effectiveness on larger models (e.g., 70B+).
Improving generalization to unseen datasets.
papers.abstract: Safety-aligned LLMs suffer from two failure modes: jailbreak (answering harmful inputs) and over-refusal (declining benign queries). Existing vector steering methods adjust the magnitude of answer vectors, but this creates a fundamental trade-off -- reducing jailbreak increases over-refusal and vice versa. We identify the root cause: LLMs encode the decision to answer (answer vector $v_a$) and the judgment of input safety (benign vector $v_b$) as nearly orthogonal directions, treating them as independent processes. We propose LLM-VA, which aligns $v_a$ with $v_b$ through closed-form weight updates, making the model's willingness to answer causally dependent on its safety assessment -- without fine-tuning or architectural changes. Our method identifies vectors at each layer using SVMs, selects safety-relevant layers, and iteratively aligns vectors via minimum-norm weight modifications. Experiments on 12 LLMs demonstrate that LLM-VA achieves 11.45% higher F1 than the best baseline while preserving 95.92% utility, and automatically adapts to each model's safety bias without manual tuning. Code and models are available at https://hotbento.github.io/LLM-VA-Web/.

papers.title: SABER: Uncovering Vulnerabilities in Safety Alignment via Cross-Layer Residual Connection
papers.research_question: How can safety alignment in Large Language Models be bypassed by exploiting the layer-wise distribution of safety mechanisms and using cross-layer residual connections?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SABER, a white-box jailbreak method that uses a cross-layer residual connection to bypass safety alignment in LLMs by routing information around safety-enforcing middle-to-late layers.
papers.conclusion: SABER is an effective jailbreak method that highlights a critical vulnerability in open-source language models to subtle architectural perturbations, demonstrating that safety alignment can be circumvented via cross-layer residual connections.
papers.key_findings:
Safety mechanisms in LLMs are predominantly embedded in the middle-to-late layers.
SABER achieves up to a 51% improvement in Attack Success Rate over the best-performing baseline on the HarmBench test set.
SABER induces only a marginal shift in perplexity on benign inputs, preserving general language capabilities.
Euclidean norm-based scaling is a critical component for SABER's effectiveness.
SABER creates an alternative pathway that reduces denial responses without significantly increasing hallucinations, balancing attack success and output coherence.
papers.limitation: The outcome when more than one layer is connected is still unexplored.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) with safe-alignment training are powerful instruments with robust language comprehension capabilities. These models typically undergo meticulous alignment procedures involving human feedback to ensure the acceptance of safe inputs while rejecting harmful or unsafe ones. However, despite their massive scale and alignment efforts, LLMs remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, where malicious users manipulate the model to produce harmful outputs that it was explicitly trained to avoid. In this study, we find that the safety mechanisms in LLMs are predominantly embedded in the middle-to-late layers. Building on this insight, we introduce a novel white-box jailbreak method, SABER (Safety Alignment Bypass via Extra Residuals), which connects two intermediate layers $s$ and $e$ such that $s < e$, through a residual connection. Our approach achieves a 51% improvement over the best-performing baseline on the HarmBench test set. Furthermore, SABER induces only a marginal shift in perplexity when evaluated on the HarmBench validation set. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/PalGitts/SABER.

papers.title: When the Coffee Feature Activates on Coffins: An Analysis of Feature Extraction and Steering for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: Does the approach of semantic feature extraction via sparse autoencoders (SAEs) offer a promising route for AI safety, and how generalizable are the claims about interpretable features and feature steering made by Anthropic?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that while sparse autoencoder (SAE)-based feature extraction and steering can produce compelling demonstrations, the methods exhibit substantial fragility and context-dependence, falling short of the systematic reliability required for safety-critical applications.
papers.conclusion: Current SAE-based interpretability methods are not reliable enough for safety-critical applications, suggesting a necessary shift in focus from prioritizing interpretability of internal representations toward reliable prediction and control of model output.
papers.key_findings:
Feature steering is fragile, with sensitivity to layer selection, steering magnitude, and context.
There exist non-standard activation behaviors (e.g., high activation density, disproportionate activation on the beginning-of-text token) that are not captured by automated feature interpretations.
It is difficult to distinguish thematically similar features from one another, even within the same layer.
Automated interpretations of features (labels) often do not align with the features' activation patterns across text samples or their effects when used for model steering.
SAE-based interpretability produces compelling demonstrations in selected cases but current methods often lack systematic reliability.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to one publicly available model (Llama 3.1-8B) and a specific set of pre-trained SAEs (Llama Scope).
The study does not have internal access to Anthropic's proprietary models (e.g., Claude 3.0 Sonnet) and relies on the assumption of a weak form of universality.
future_direction: Future work should focus on reliable prediction and control of model output, rather than just interpretability of internal representations.
More research is needed to understand the conditions under which interpretable features emerge and to verify that they function computationally in ways analogous to human concepts.
papers.abstract: Recent work by Anthropic on Mechanistic interpretability claims to understand and control Large Language Models by extracting human-interpretable features from their neural activation patterns using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). If successful, this approach offers one of the most promising routes for human oversight in AI safety. We conduct an initial stress-test of these claims by replicating their main results with open-source SAEs for Llama 3.1. While we successfully reproduce basic feature extraction and steering capabilities, our investigation suggests that major caution is warranted regarding the generalizability of these claims. We find that feature steering exhibits substantial fragility, with sensitivity to layer selection, steering magnitude, and context. We observe non-standard activation behavior and demonstrate the difficulty to distinguish thematically similar features from one another. While SAE-based interpretability produces compelling demonstrations in selected cases, current methods often fall short of the systematic reliability required for safety-critical applications. This suggests a necessary shift in focus from prioritizing interpretability of internal representations toward reliable prediction and control of model output. Our work contributes to a more nuanced understanding of what mechanistic interpretability has achieved and highlights fundamental challenges for AI safety that remain unresolved.

papers.title: Forbidden Facts: An Investigation of Competing Objectives in Llama-2
papers.research_question: How do models resolve competing objectives? Specifically, how does Llama-2 suppress the correct answer when instructed not to say it in the forbidden fact task?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that the suppression behavior in Llama-2 is implemented by a heterogeneous set of around 35 components that use faulty heuristics, which can be exploited via an adversarial attack (California Attack), suggesting challenges for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The mechanisms used by Llama-2 are complex and heterogeneous, indicating that even simple behaviors are implemented in complicated ways, which may make interpretability goals difficult to achieve.
papers.key_findings:
Around 35 residual stream components are responsible for the suppression behavior in the forbidden fact task.
These components are heterogeneous in their attention patterns and suppression mechanisms.
The most important attention heads attend to the forbidden token and have suppressive OV circuits.
The attention mechanism is not semantically or positionally specific.
An adversarial attack (California Attack) can exploit these heuristics to cause incorrect answers.
papers.limitation:
The mechanisms are complex and heterogeneous, making them hard to interpret.
The California Attack shows the model's heuristics are faulty and not robust.
future_direction: Decompose MLPs and use sparse probing and autoencoders to interpret features from individual neurons.
Explore whether there exists a 'basis' in which LLM behavior is easier to understand.
papers.abstract: LLMs often face competing pressures (for example helpfulness vs. harmlessness). To understand how models resolve such conflicts, we study Llama-2-chat models on the forbidden fact task. Specifically, we instruct Llama-2 to truthfully complete a factual recall statement while forbidding it from saying the correct answer. This often makes the model give incorrect answers. We decompose Llama-2 into 1000+ components, and rank each one with respect to how useful it is for forbidding the correct answer. We find that in aggregate, around 35 components are enough to reliably implement the full suppression behavior. However, these components are fairly heterogeneous and many operate using faulty heuristics. We discover that one of these heuristics can be exploited via a manually designed adversarial attack which we call The California Attack. Our results highlight some roadblocks standing in the way of being able to successfully interpret advanced ML systems. Project website available at https://forbiddenfacts.github.io .

papers.title: SAFER: Probing Safety in Reward Models with Sparse Autoencoder
papers.research_question: Can we interpret reward model decisions? Can we understand the influence of preference data on reward models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAFER, a framework that uses sparse autoencoders to interpret reward models by extracting safety-relevant features, enabling targeted data manipulation for precise safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: SAFER provides a practical tool for interpreting reward models and performing precise, feature-guided manipulation of preference data, enhancing the transparency and controllability of safety alignment.
papers.key_findings:
SAFER identifies human-interpretable, monosemantic features in reward model activations that are strongly associated with safety.
Using feature-level scores, SAFER enables precise data poisoning that significantly degrades safety alignment with minimal impact on general chat performance.
SAFER also enables effective data denoising, improving safety alignment by removing low-quality preference pairs.
GPT-4o's safety relevance ratings show high alignment with human judgments, validating its use as an automated evaluator.
Ablation studies confirm the importance of safety-oriented fine-tuning and sentence-level representation for effective feature extraction.
papers.limitation:
Generalization to other alignment dimensions beyond safety (e.g., reasoning, helpfulness) remains an open question.
Experiments are conducted on relatively small-scale models; evaluation on larger models is needed.
future_direction: Explore the application of SAFER to other alignment dimensions beyond safety (e.g., reasoning, helpfulness).
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is a key paradigm for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human values, yet the reward models at its core remain largely opaque. In this work, we present Sparse Autoencoder For Enhanced Reward model (\textbf{SAFER}), a novel framework for interpreting and improving reward models through mechanistic analysis. Leveraging Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), we uncover human-interpretable features in reward model activations, enabling insight into safety-relevant decision-making. We apply SAFER to safety-oriented preference datasets and quantify the salience of individual features by activation differences between chosen and rejected responses. Using these feature-level signals, we design targeted data poisoning and denoising strategies. Experiments show that SAFER can precisely degrade or enhance safety alignment with minimal data modification, without sacrificing general chat performance. Our approach contributes to interpreting, auditing and refining reward models in high-stakes LLM alignment tasks. Our codes are available at https://github.com/xzy-101/SAFER-code. \textit{This paper discusses topics related to reward model safety and may include discussions or examples that highlight potential risks or unsafe outcomes.}

papers.title: Refusal Direction is Universal Across Safety-Aligned Languages
papers.research_question: How universal are refusal directions across languages? Specifically, does a refusal direction extracted from one language transfer to others?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that refusal directions are universal across safety-aligned languages; a refusal vector extracted from one language can effectively modulate refusal behavior in other languages.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that refusal directions are universal across safety-aligned languages, providing insights for multilingual safety defenses.
papers.key_findings:
English-derived refusal vectors can jailbreak models across multiple languages.
Refusal vectors derived from any safety-aligned language (e.g., German, Chinese, Thai) transfer to other languages.
The universality is due to parallelism of refusal vectors across languages in the embedding space.
Models fail to separate harmful and harmless prompts in non-English languages, leading to vulnerabilities.
Adding refusal vectors can reduce compliance rates, demonstrating controllability.
papers.abstract: Refusal mechanisms in large language models (LLMs) are essential for ensuring safety. Recent research has revealed that refusal behavior can be mediated by a single direction in activation space, enabling targeted interventions to bypass refusals. While this is primarily demonstrated in an English-centric context, appropriate refusal behavior is important for any language, but poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the refusal behavior in LLMs across 14 languages using PolyRefuse, a multilingual safety dataset created by translating malicious and benign English prompts into these languages. We uncover the surprising cross-lingual universality of the refusal direction: a vector extracted from English can bypass refusals in other languages with near-perfect effectiveness, without any additional fine-tuning. Even more remarkably, refusal directions derived from any safety-aligned language transfer seamlessly to others. We attribute this transferability to the parallelism of refusal vectors across languages in the embedding space and identify the underlying mechanism behind cross-lingual jailbreaks. These findings provide actionable insights for building more robust multilingual safety defenses and pave the way for a deeper mechanistic understanding of cross-lingual vulnerabilities in LLMs.

papers.title: Feature-Guided SAE Steering for Refusal-Rate Control using Contrasting Prompts
papers.research_question: How can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be used with a systematic feature selection method to steer large language models for improved safety (refusal rate) without sacrificing utility?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using contrasting prompts and a composite scoring function to systematically select Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features for steering, achieving simultaneous safety and utility improvements on Llama-3 8B without model retraining.
papers.conclusion: Feature-guided SAE steering is a viable and efficient approach to improving LLM safety without sacrificing utility, providing a foundation for mechanistically-informed safety alignment.
papers.key_findings:
A composite scoring method using contrasting prompts can identify SAE features causally related to refusal behavior.
Steering the top-ranked feature (Feature 35831) improved safety performance by 18.9% and utility by 11.1%, overcoming the traditional safety-utility tradeoff.
The method provides a computationally efficient alternative to traditional safety alignment methods like RLHF and Constitutional AI, which require extensive retraining.
papers.limitation:
The evaluation is restricted to Llama-3 8B and Layer 25, limiting understanding of scaling behaviors across architectures and transformer depths.
Reliance on automatic judges (GPT-4o for AirBench, GPT-4 for AlpacaEval 2.0) introduces potential limitations despite demonstrated correlation with human preferences.
The absence of direct comparisons with alternative steering methods limits the ability to establish relative effectiveness claims.
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) deployment requires guiding the LLM to recognize and not answer unsafe prompts while complying with safe prompts. Previous methods for achieving this require adjusting model weights along with other expensive procedures. While recent advances in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have enabled interpretable feature extraction from LLMs, existing approaches lack systematic feature selection methods and principled evaluation of safety-utility tradeoffs. We explored using different steering features and steering strengths using Sparse Auto Encoders (SAEs) to provide a solution. Using an accurate and innovative contrasting prompt method with the AI-Generated Prompts Dataset from teknium/OpenHermes-2p5-Mistral-7B and Air Bench eu-dataset to efficiently choose the best features in the model to steer, we tested this method on Llama-3 8B. We conclude that using this method, our approach achieves an 18.9% improvement in safety performance while simultaneously increasing utility by 11.1%, demonstrating that targeted SAE steering can overcome traditional safety-utility tradeoffs when optimal features are identified through principled selection methods.

papers.title: GSAE: Graph-Regularized Sparse Autoencoders for Robust LLM Safety Steering
papers.research_question: How to effectively steer LLMs for safety by capturing distributed safety representations using graph-regularized sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Graph-Regularized Sparse Autoencoders (GSAE) to capture distributed safety representations in LLMs, enabling effective runtime safety steering with high refusal rates and preserved utility.
papers.conclusion: GSAE provides a robust method for safety steering by learning distributed safety representations, achieving high safety discrimination and utility preservation across diverse models and attacks.
papers.key_findings:
GSAE steering achieves an average 82% selective refusal rate, substantially outperforming standard SAE steering (42%).
It maintains strong task accuracy on QA benchmarks (e.g., 70% on TriviaQA, 65% on TruthfulQA, 74% on GSM8K).
GSAE generalizes across multiple LLM families (LLaMA-3, Mistral, Qwen, Phi) and scales.
It is robust against jailbreak attacks (GCG, AutoDAN), consistently maintaining ≥90% refusal of harmful content.
Ablation studies show that graph regularization is essential for performance, and the dual-gating mechanism enables adaptive steering.
papers.limitation: The runtime steering mechanism incurs inference latency overhead, which can interfere with optimized serving engines.
future_direction: Decomposing distributed features into interpretable safety sub-categories.
Ensuring the robustness of the neuron co-activation graph to dataset biases and adversarial inputs.
Extending graph-regularized learning to multi-modal domains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) face critical safety challenges, as they can be manipulated to generate harmful content through adversarial prompts and jailbreak attacks. Many defenses are typically either black-box guardrails that filter outputs, or internals-based methods that steer hidden activations by operationalizing safety as a single latent feature or dimension. While effective for simple concepts, this assumption is limiting, as recent evidence shows that abstract concepts such as refusal and temporality are distributed across multiple features rather than isolated in one. To address this limitation, we introduce Graph-Regularized Sparse Autoencoders (GSAEs), which extends SAEs with a Laplacian smoothness penalty on the neuron co-activation graph. Unlike standard SAEs that assign each concept to a single latent feature, GSAEs recover smooth, distributed safety representations as coherent patterns spanning multiple features. We empirically demonstrate that GSAE enables effective runtime safety steering, assembling features into a weighted set of safety-relevant directions and controlling them with a two-stage gating mechanism that activates interventions only when harmful prompts or continuations are detected during generation. This approach enforces refusals adaptively while preserving utility on benign queries. Across safety and QA benchmarks, GSAE steering achieves an average 82% selective refusal rate, substantially outperforming standard SAE steering (42%), while maintaining strong task accuracy (70% on TriviaQA, 65% on TruthfulQA, 74% on GSM8K). Robustness experiments further show generalization across LLaMA-3, Mistral, Qwen, and Phi families and resilience against jailbreak attacks (GCG, AutoDAN), consistently maintaining >= 90% refusal of harmful content.

papers.title: Compact Proofs of Model Performance via Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability be used to derive compact formal guarantees on model performance? Does more compact proof require and provide more mechanistic understanding, and does more faithful understanding lead to tighter bounds?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability can be used to generate compact formal proofs of model performance, and shows that more compact proofs require more mechanistic understanding and that more faithful understanding leads to tighter bounds.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability can be used to generate compact proofs of model performance, but compounding structureless errors pose a challenge that future work must address.
papers.key_findings:
Shorter proofs seem to require and provide more mechanistic understanding.
More faithful mechanistic understanding leads to tighter performance bounds.
Compounding structureless errors is a key challenge for using mechanistic interpretability to generate compact proofs on model performance.
papers.limitation:
Compounding structureless errors pose a challenge for generating compact proofs.
The approach is demonstrated only on a simple toy setting (Max-of-K).
future_direction: Addressing the challenge of compounding structureless errors in generating compact proofs.
Extending the approach to more complex tasks and models.
papers.abstract: We propose using mechanistic interpretability -- techniques for reverse engineering model weights into human-interpretable algorithms -- to derive and compactly prove formal guarantees on model performance. We prototype this approach by formally proving accuracy lower bounds for a small transformer trained on Max-of-K, validating proof transferability across 151 random seeds and four values of K. We create 102 different computer-assisted proof strategies and assess their length and tightness of bound on each of our models. Using quantitative metrics, we find that shorter proofs seem to require and provide more mechanistic understanding. Moreover, we find that more faithful mechanistic understanding leads to tighter performance bounds. We confirm these connections by qualitatively examining a subset of our proofs. Finally, we identify compounding structureless errors as a key challenge for using mechanistic interpretability to generate compact proofs on model performance.

papers.title: Learning Safety Constraints for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we learn and enforce safety constraints in large language models via a geometric polytope in the model's representation space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SaP, a geometric framework that learns safety constraints as a polytope in the LLM's representation space, enabling post-hoc safety steering and interpretable insights into safety concepts.
papers.conclusion: The geometric perspective of safety constraints offers a promising framework for aligning and controlling model behaviors, though further research is needed for theoretical foundations and robustness.
papers.key_findings:
SaP effectively defends against adversarial attacks while preserving model capabilities on standard benchmarks.
The learned polytope facets naturally correspond to different semantic safety concepts (e.g., violence, misinformation).
The concept encoder reduces polysemanticity in the learned features, improving interpretability and defense performance.
SaP's geometric approach provides a more structured and effective safety model compared to MLP-based classifiers.
The method operates post-hoc without model fine-tuning, preserving original model weights.
papers.limitation:
The heuristic facet assignment algorithm limits overall performance.
Under many attacks, specifically for the Ministral-8B model, SaP can induce semantically incoherent outputs.
Lacks a rigorous theoretical understanding and formal guarantees for safety in large-scale models.
future_direction: Further disentangling semantic understandings across polytope edges, possibly using mechanistic interpretability or non-linear geometric representations.
Improving SaP's performance in adversarial robustness and broad capability domains.
Adapting theoretical sample complexity bounds for learning polytopes to the context of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful tools but pose significant safety risks through harmful outputs and vulnerability to adversarial attacks. We propose SaP, short for Safety Polytope, a geometric approach to LLM safety that learns and enforces multiple safety constraints directly in the model's representation space. We develop a framework that identifies safe and unsafe regions via the polytope's facets, enabling both detection and correction of unsafe outputs through geometric steering. Unlike existing approaches that modify model weights, SaP operates post-hoc in the representation space, preserving model capabilities while enforcing safety constraints. Experiments across multiple LLMs demonstrate that our method can effectively detect unethical inputs, reduce adversarial attack success rates while maintaining performance on standard tasks, thus highlighting the importance of having an explicit geometric model for safety. Analysis of the learned polytope facets reveals emergence of specialization in detecting different semantic notions of safety, providing interpretable insights into how safety is captured in LLMs' representation space.

papers.title: Seeing It or Not? Interpretable Vision-aware Latent Steering to Mitigate Object Hallucinations
papers.research_question: How do visual inputs influence the decision-making processes of Large Vision-Language Models, and how can we use this understanding to mitigate object hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces VaLSe, a vision-aware latent steering framework that uses interpretable visual contribution maps to trace visual influence on token generation and then steers internal representations to mitigate object hallucinations in LVLMs.
papers.conclusion: VaLSe effectively mitigates object hallucinations and provides interpretable insights into model decision-making, while also revealing limitations in current OH benchmarks and advocating for more nuanced evaluation.
papers.key_findings:
VaLSe reduces object hallucination metrics (CS, CI) on multiple benchmarks while preserving general task performance.
Visual contribution maps show that models may generate correct answers while attending to irrelevant image regions, indicating reliance on language priors.
Existing OH metrics like CHAIR sometimes flag visually grounded and accurate descriptions as hallucinations, indicating limitations in current evaluation.
The method can identify potential reasons for hallucinations, such as attention to misleading visual cues (e.g., logos leading to 'cell phone' hallucination).
Latent steering using SVD-derived directions effectively shifts model focus to semantically relevant image content.
papers.limitation:
VaLSe is less effective on models with complex vision encoders like Qwen2-VL due to difficulty in tracing visual token influence.
Limited improvement on multiple-choice question formats (e.g., MMVP benchmark).
future_direction: Developing more nuanced, interpretable, and visually grounded benchmarks for object hallucination evaluation.
Incorporating interpretability more critically in future hallucination mitigation research.
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved remarkable success but continue to struggle with object hallucination (OH), generating outputs inconsistent with visual inputs. While previous work has proposed methods to reduce OH, the visual decision-making mechanisms that lead to hallucinations remain poorly understood. In this paper, we propose VaLSe, a Vision-aware Latent Steering framework that adopts an interpretation-then-mitigation strategy to address OH in LVLMs. By tackling dual challenges of modeling complex vision-language interactions and eliminating spurious activation artifacts, VaLSe can generate visual contribution maps that trace how specific visual inputs influence individual output tokens. These maps reveal the model's vision-aware focus regions, which are then used to perform latent space steering, realigning internal representations toward semantically relevant content and reducing hallucinated outputs. Extensive experiments demonstrate that VaLSe is a powerful interpretability tool and an effective method for enhancing model robustness against OH across multiple benchmarks. Furthermore, our analysis uncovers limitations in existing OH evaluation metrics, underscoring the need for more nuanced, interpretable, and visually grounded OH benchmarks in future work. Code is available at: https://github.com/Ziwei-Zheng/VaLSe.

papers.title: Towards Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we automate the discovery of circuits in neural networks for mechanistic interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper systematizes the mechanistic interpretability workflow and introduces the ACDC algorithm to automate circuit discovery by using activation patching to find important connections in the computational graph.
papers.conclusion: ACDC is a step towards automating circuit discovery in mechanistic interpretability, showing promise on several tasks but with limitations that need to be addressed in future work.
papers.key_findings:
ACDC successfully rediscovers known circuits, such as the Greater-Than circuit in GPT-2 Small and the IOI circuit.
ACDC selects a sparse set of edges (e.g., 68 out of 32,000 in GPT-2 Small for IOI) that match manually found circuits.
ACDC performs competitively with gradient-based methods like Subnetwork Probing and Head Importance Score for Pruning.
ACDC is not robust in all settings, e.g., it fails on tracr tasks when using corrupted activations.
ACDC can miss negative components when optimizing for logit difference.
papers.limitation:
ACDC can fail in some settings, such as on tracr tasks when using corrupted activations.
ACDC may miss negative components when optimizing for logit difference.
The ground-truth circuits from previous work are not 100% reliable, limiting the evaluation.
future_direction: Automating the functional interpretation of model components.
Improving circuit discovery methods to handle more complex behaviors and models.
papers.abstract: Through considerable effort and intuition, several recent works have reverse-engineered nontrivial behaviors of transformer models. This paper systematizes the mechanistic interpretability process they followed. First, researchers choose a metric and dataset that elicit the desired model behavior. Then, they apply activation patching to find which abstract neural network units are involved in the behavior. By varying the dataset, metric, and units under investigation, researchers can understand the functionality of each component. We automate one of the process' steps: to identify the circuit that implements the specified behavior in the model's computational graph. We propose several algorithms and reproduce previous interpretability results to validate them. For example, the ACDC algorithm rediscovered 5/5 of the component types in a circuit in GPT-2 Small that computes the Greater-Than operation. ACDC selected 68 of the 32,000 edges in GPT-2 Small, all of which were manually found by previous work. Our code is available at https://github.com/ArthurConmy/Automatic-Circuit-Discovery.

papers.title: Vision-Language Introspection: Mitigating Overconfident Hallucinations in MLLMs via Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering
papers.research_question: How to mitigate overconfident hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by simulating a metacognitive self-correction process that diagnoses and rectifies internal visual-semantic misalignments?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that mitigates object hallucinations in MLLMs by first introspectively localizing causal visual anchors and then performing interpretable bi-causal steering to rectify internal representations and calibrate overconfidence.
papers.conclusion: VLI effectively mitigates overconfident hallucinations in MLLMs by introspectively diagnosing visual-semantic conflicts and actively steering internal representations towards verified visual evidence, achieving state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
VLI reduces the object hallucination rate by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improves accuracy by up to 6.33% on POPE compared to baseline models.
